sources.title: Anthropic's IPO filing sheds new light on who stands to make money from public debut - Yahoo Finance
passages: The filing also shed light on Anthropic's venture capital backers including Spark Capital, whose affiliated funds purchased approximately $777 million in preferred stock across six financing rounds between 2023 and 2026.

Anthropic's long-awaited filing on Monday offered investors a fresh glimpse into the fortunes at stake for some of the biggest names in tech and finance ahead of the artificial intelligence startup's stock market debut.
"Amazon is going to be the biggest beneficiary because it can win twice," Harrison Rolfes, a senior analyst with PitchBook, told Yahoo Finance last month.
It wins on compute sales, it wins on investment," he added.

The arrangement could be reduced by as much as $10 billion if Google exercises an option to purchase nonvoting Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the IPO, at the offering price.
Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, exceeding its sales for all of last year.
But the company also spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure during those six months, according to the filing.
The new filing details a financing agreement with Alphabet, Google's parent company ( GOOG , GOOGL ), that could provide Anthropic with up to $20 billion in additional funding.
Neither of the tech giants' facilities had been drawn as of June 30.
But Amazon and Google stand to benefit from far more than their equity investment in the startup.
Anthropic is also a major customer of Amazon Web Services, which provides cloud computing capacity and distributes the company's AI models to customers.
Spark has ties to Anthropic's board through director Yasmin Razavi, who is a general partner at the investment firm.
Other investors in Anthropic have included Menlo Ventures, Coatue Management and Lightspeed Venture Partners, as well as funds managed by Fidelity and Blackstone.
The carrying value of Amazon's various Anthropic investments totaled $190.4 billion, according to a July disclosure.
Anthropic facilitated an April tender offer in which shareholders sold approximately $4.66 billion in stock.
The maker of Claude is preparing for a potential November listing that could rival SpaceX's ( SPCX ) debut as the largest IPO in history.

Anthropic's long-awaited filing on Monday offered investors a fresh glimpse into the fortunes at stake for some of the biggest names in tech and finance ahead of the artificial intelligence startup's stock market debut. The arrangement could be reduced by as much as $10 billion if Google exercises an option to purchase nonvoting Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the IPO, at the offering price. Google's financing agreement carries a 14.99% ownership cap, which the company can waive. No funds had been drawn under the arrangement as of June 30, according to the filing. Amazon ( AMZN ), one of Anthropic's other biggest backers, holds approximately $6.2 billion in outstanding convertible notes that could become roughly 1.84 billion nonvoting shares when the AI startup completes its IPO, according to the filing. The conversion is subject to a 12% ownership cap, which Amazon can waive. Any notes that cannot convert because of the restriction would remain outstanding and could convert into additional shares following the offering. The carrying value of Amazon's various Anthropic investments totaled $190.4 billion, according to a July disclosure. Amazon has separately agreed to provide up to $15 billion in additional financing tied to Anthropic hitting computing capacity milestones. Neither of the tech giants' facilities had been drawn as of June 30. But Amazon and Google stand to benefit from far more than their equity investment in the startup. Anthropic is also a major customer of Amazon Web Services, which provides cloud computing capacity and distributes the company's AI models to customers. Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, exceeding its sales for all of last year. But the company also spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure during those six months, according to the filing. The AI developer has also committed to spending roughly $450 billion on cloud computing in the coming years, including agreements with Amazon and Google. "Amazon is going to be the biggest beneficiary because it can win twice," Harrison Rolfes, a senior analyst with PitchBook, told Yahoo Finance last month. It wins on compute sales, it wins on investment," he added. Both tech giants report third quarter earnings later this week. The filing also shed light on Anthropic's venture capital backers including Spark Capital, whose affiliated funds purchased approximately $777 million in preferred stock across six financing rounds between 2023 and 2026. Spark has ties to Anthropic's board through director Yasmin Razavi, who is a general partner at the investment firm. Other investors in Anthropic have included Menlo Ventures, Coatue Management and Lightspeed Venture Partners, as well as funds managed by Fidelity and Blackstone. Some shareholders have already converted part of their holdings into cash ahead of the IPO. Anthropic facilitated an April tender offer in which shareholders sold approximately $4.66 billion in stock. Participants included CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and other executives, although the filing did not disclose how much each received. The prospectus did not specify Amazon's, Alphabet's or other major institutional investors' ownership percentages in its principal stockholders table, which instead identified founders and special voting-rights holders. Anthropic's founders will retain 50.1% of the company's voting power following the IPO through a separate share class, while a trust will have the right to elect a majority of directors. passages: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, as the AI giant detailed in a post on its website .

Anthropic said the number of shares and prices for them "have not yet been determined," but the IPO could value the AI company at around $2 trillion when the stock is expected to debut in mid-November.

extraction.body: The company may be valued as high as $2 trillion. Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, as the AI giant detailed in a post on its website . The company sent its Form S-1 to the Securities and Exchange Commission, confirming that the stock would be listed on Nasdaq under "ANT." Anthropic previously filed a draft version of its S-1 form with the SEC in June. Anthropic said the number of shares and prices for them "have not yet been determined," but the IPO could value the AI company at around $2 trillion when the stock is expected to debut in mid-November. In its filing, Anthropic said that "as of June 30, 2026, we had raised an aggregate of $141.1 billion of capital and had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion and short-term investments of $19.3 billion." Charting the company's rapid growth, Anthropic's filing also detailed that its revenue grew 1,368 percent year-over-year for the three months ending in June 30, 2026, offset by a 300 percent growth in its compute and infrastructure expenses during that same time frame. However, Anthropic's draft filing from June revealed some more context as the company reported an operating loss of $8 billion last year. As one of the leading companies in the industry, Anthropic has also advocated for slowing down the AI race. Dario Amodei, the company's CEO, published a three-step plan looking to curb AI's concerning rate of development. The Anthropic IPO filing mentions four categories of risk related to dangers of AI, including misuse, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. The company claimed that a highly capable frontier AI model which could exceed the cognitive capabilities of top human experts, navigate all interfaces of a human working virtually and interact with the physical world through lab equipment and robotic systems would "become widely available within a few years." Anthropic concludes its pitch to investors by saying its goal is "to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery and bring forth an age of miracles."

sources.title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
passages: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.
After weeks of leaked S-1s , Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.
Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt.
The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business.

As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.
Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing. That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more. As previously reported , Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing. Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board. The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price. coreStoryFacts.text: Elon Musk’s SpaceX — which owns xAI and also has a newly minted deal with Anthropic that has the latter paying $15 billion per year to use SpaceX data centers — is currently set to raise $80 billion in its public debut, which would make it the largest IPO in history.

Anthropic chose to submit its draft registration statement to the SEC confidentially, according to a blog post from the company, meaning key details typically included in that form about a company’s operations — like potential risks to its business, executive compensation, and other financials — won’t become public until later on in the process.
As of its fundraise last week, Anthropic is being called the world’s most valuable startup, with a post-money valuation of $965 billion.
After months of speculation about whether OpenAI or Anthropic would be first in their race to IPO, Anthropic on Monday reached a key milestone: filing to kick off the process with the U.S.

The filing also shed light on Anthropic's venture capital backers including Spark Capital, whose affiliated funds purchased approximately $777 million in preferred stock across six financing rounds between 2023 and 2026.

Anthropic's long-awaited filing on Monday offered investors a fresh glimpse into the fortunes at stake for some of the biggest names in tech and finance ahead of the artificial intelligence startup's stock market debut.
"Amazon is going to be the biggest beneficiary because it can win twice," Harrison Rolfes, a senior analyst with PitchBook, told Yahoo Finance last month.
It wins on compute sales, it wins on investment," he added.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The arrangement could be reduced by as much as $10 billion if Google exercises an option to purchase nonvoting Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the IPO, at the offering price.
Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, exceeding its sales for all of last year.
But the company also spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure during those six months, according to the filing.
The new filing details a financing agreement with Alphabet, Google's parent company ( GOOG , GOOGL ), that could provide Anthropic with up to $20 billion in additional funding.
Neither of the tech giants' facilities had been drawn as of June 30.
But Amazon and Google stand to benefit from far more than their equity investment in the startup.
Anthropic is also a major customer of Amazon Web Services, which provides cloud computing capacity and distributes the company's AI models to customers.
Spark has ties to Anthropic's board through director Yasmin Razavi, who is a general partner at the investment firm.
Other investors in Anthropic have included Menlo Ventures, Coatue Management and Lightspeed Venture Partners, as well as funds managed by Fidelity and Blackstone.
The carrying value of Amazon's various Anthropic investments totaled $190.4 billion, according to a July disclosure.
Anthropic facilitated an April tender offer in which shareholders sold approximately $4.66 billion in stock.
The maker of Claude is preparing for a potential November listing that could rival SpaceX's ( SPCX ) debut as the largest IPO in history.

Anthropic said the number of shares and prices for them "have not yet been determined," but the IPO could value the AI company at around $2 trillion when the stock is expected to debut in mid-November.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.

passages: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, as the AI giant detailed in a post on its website .

extraction.body: The company may be valued as high as $2 trillion. Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, as the AI giant detailed in a post on its website . The company sent its Form S-1 to the Securities and Exchange Commission, confirming that the stock would be listed on Nasdaq under "ANT." Anthropic previously filed a draft version of its S-1 form with the SEC in June. Anthropic said the number of shares and prices for them "have not yet been determined," but the IPO could value the AI company at around $2 trillion when the stock is expected to debut in mid-November. In its filing, Anthropic said that "as of June 30, 2026, we had raised an aggregate of $141.1 billion of capital and had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion and short-term investments of $19.3 billion." Charting the company's rapid growth, Anthropic's filing also detailed that its revenue grew 1,368 percent year-over-year for the three months ending in June 30, 2026, offset by a 300 percent growth in its compute and infrastructure expenses during that same time frame. However, Anthropic's draft filing from June revealed some more context as the company reported an operating loss of $8 billion last year. As one of the leading companies in the industry, Anthropic has also advocated for slowing down the AI race. Dario Amodei, the company's CEO, published a three-step plan looking to curb AI's concerning rate of development. The Anthropic IPO filing mentions four categories of risk related to dangers of AI, including misuse, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. The company claimed that a highly capable frontier AI model which could exceed the cognitive capabilities of top human experts, navigate all interfaces of a human working virtually and interact with the physical world through lab equipment and robotic systems would "become widely available within a few years." Anthropic concludes its pitch to investors by saying its goal is "to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery and bring forth an age of miracles."

sources.title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
passages: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.
After weeks of leaked S-1s , Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.
Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt.
The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business.

As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.
Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing. That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more. As previously reported , Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing. Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board. The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price. sources.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push - CNBC
passages: Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter.
The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.
Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies.
In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for.
Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees .

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees .
But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan.
The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.
The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile.
In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.
Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec.
Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation , increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use.
It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results .
At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.
WATCH: Amazon, Microsoft earnings key to gauging AI investment returns: CIO
On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.

passages: Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter.
The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.
Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies.
In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for.
Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees .

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees .
But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan.
The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.
The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile.
In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.
Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec.
Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation , increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use.
It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results .
At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.

On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.

coreStoryFacts.text: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 workers, according to a report by Bloomberg .
The company employs approximately 223,000 people , so this would constitute over a quarter of the global workforce.
It is worth reiterating that this is a voluntary buyout program.
That 60,000 number sounds huge, and it is, but we don't know how many people will accept the terms.
Microsoft did something similar earlier this year and only 30 percent of eligible workers signed on the dotted line.

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,"...
Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter.
The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.
Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies.
In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for.
Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees .

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees .
But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan.
The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.
The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile.
In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.
Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec.
Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation , increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use.
It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results .
At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.

In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses. In a follow-up post , he added that the financing primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, which are expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027. In a regulatory filing Monday, SpaceX said it signed a binding commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for roughly $40 billion in GPU financing. The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models. SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI. The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release. Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. He predicted that more than 200 so-called neocloud companies, which provide cloud computing infrastructure designed for AI and machine-learning workloads, would face widespread failures and consolidation, with only a small number surviving. In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses. In a follow-up post , he added that the financing primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, which are expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027. In a regulatory filing Monday, SpaceX said it signed a binding commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for roughly $40 billion in GPU financing. The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models. SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI. The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release. Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. passages: SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.

In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses.
In a follow-up post , he added that the financing primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, which are expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027.
In a regulatory filing Monday, SpaceX said it signed a binding commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for roughly $40 billion in GPU financing.

The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.
SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI.
The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release.
Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

He predicted that more than 200 so-called neocloud companies, which provide cloud computing infrastructure designed for AI and machine-learning workloads, would face widespread failures and consolidation, with only a small number surviving.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.
The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.
The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

extraction.body: SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday . SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” in a statement. Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing. SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive. The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets. “This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services. Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.” The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses. The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business . SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined. Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s Oct. 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone. The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits. Elon Musk's SpaceX announced a $40 billion AI hardware financing agreement on October 26, bringing Apollo Global Management, Goldman Sachs and other major Wall Street investors into one of the largest computing infrastructure deals ever disclosed. Under the official agreement , an Apollo-managed entity will purchase Nvidia GPUs and related equipment before leasing them to SpaceX. The arrangement will finance next-generation Vera Rubin chips for the company's growing terrestrial computing infrastructure. The agreement confirms earlier financing negotiations , although the master lease remains subject to closing conditions. SpaceX expects to finalize it before the end of 2026, with equipment deliveries and lease payments beginning in the first half of 2027. Rather than purchasing $40 billion of Nvidia equipment entirely with its own cash, SpaceX will lease hardware acquired by the Apollo-managed financing entity. Each equipment tranche will carry a lease lasting approximately five to five-and-a-quarter years. Quarterly principal payments will generally equal one-twentieth of the financed equipment cost, with additional interest and expenses. The interest rate has not yet been determined. Apollo and Goldman Sachs are leading the financing, with Goldman acting as sole structuring agent. Funds managed by BlackRock and Goldman Sachs Asset Management, alongside KKR-advised capital accounts, have also made anchor commitments. The transaction illustrates how AI infrastructure borrowing is evolving beyond conventional corporate loans and bonds. It also gives SpaceX access to additional hardware without requiring the entire purchase amount upfront, although the company still assumes substantial multiyear payment obligations. SpaceX is no longer primarily a rocket-launch and satellite-connectivity business. Its Super Intelligence division generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue, surpassing the $5.25 billion reported by its connectivity division, which includes Starlink. That AI revenue expansion helps explain the company's appetite for additional computing capacity. Management expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of $35 billion-$40 billion as investment in infrastructure accelerates. The company is also selling computing capacity to outside customers. An earlier Reflection AI agreement demonstrated how its Colossus facilities could generate revenue beyond supporting Grok models. The new hardware will use Nvidia's Vera Rubin architecture, extending a technology relationship already central to SpaceX's computing strategy . SpaceX executives claim some infrastructure investments can pay for themselves in less than one year. However, such expectations depend on utilization, operating costs and customers continuing to purchase computing capacity. The timing is particularly significant because financing conditions have deteriorated for specialized AI cloud providers. Musk recently warned that more than 200 neocloud companies could face widespread consolidation or failure as lenders become increasingly reluctant to finance businesses dependent almost entirely on AI infrastructure revenue. Unlike many smaller cloud providers, SpaceX benefits from established rocket-launch and Starlink operations. Musk argues that this diversified revenue supports its access to investment-grade financing. That advantage contrasts with the pressure facing CoreWeave and Nebius , whose borrowing costs and stock valuations have come under scrutiny. Elon Musk's SpaceX announced a $40 billion AI hardware financing agreement on October 26, bringing Apollo Global Management, Goldman Sachs and other major Wall Street investors into one of the largest computing infrastructure deals ever disclosed.

Under the official agreement , an Apollo-managed entity will purchase Nvidia GPUs and related equipment before leasing them to SpaceX. The arrangement will finance next-generation Vera Rubin chips for the company's growing terrestrial computing infrastructure.

The agreement confirms earlier financing negotiations , although the master lease remains subject to closing conditions. SpaceX expects to finalize it before the end of 2026, with equipment deliveries and lease payments beginning in the first half of 2027.
Rather than purchasing $40 billion of Nvidia equipment entirely with its own cash, SpaceX will lease hardware acquired by the Apollo-managed financing entity.

Each equipment tranche will carry a lease lasting approximately five to five-and-a-quarter years. Quarterly principal payments will generally equal one-twentieth of the financed equipment cost, with additional interest and expenses. The interest rate has not yet been determined.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs are leading the financing, with Goldman acting as sole structuring agent. Funds managed by BlackRock and Goldman Sachs Asset Management, alongside KKR-advised capital accounts, have also made anchor commitments.
The transaction illustrates how AI infrastructure borrowing is evolving beyond conventional corporate loans and bonds.
It also gives SpaceX access to additional hardware without requiring the entire purchase amount upfront, although the company still assumes substantial multiyear payment obligations.
SpaceX is no longer primarily a rocket-launch and satellite-connectivity business.

Its Super Intelligence division generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue, surpassing the $5.25 billion reported by its connectivity division, which includes Starlink. That AI revenue expansion helps explain the company's appetite for additional computing capacity.
Management expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of $35 billion-$40 billion as investment in infrastructure accelerates.
The company is also selling computing capacity to outside customers. An earlier Reflection AI agreement demonstrated how its Colossus facilities could generate revenue beyond supporting Grok models.
The new hardware will use Nvidia's Vera Rubin architecture, extending a technology relationship already central to SpaceX's computing strategy .

SpaceX executives claim some infrastructure investments can pay for themselves in less than one year. However, such expectations depend on utilization, operating costs and customers continuing to purchase computing capacity.
The timing is particularly significant because financing conditions have deteriorated for specialized AI cloud providers.

Musk recently warned that more than 200 neocloud companies could face widespread consolidation or failure as lenders become increasingly reluctant to finance businesses dependent almost entirely on AI infrastructure revenue.

Unlike many smaller cloud providers, SpaceX benefits from established rocket-launch and Starlink operations. Musk argues that this diversified revenue supports its access to investment-grade financing.
That advantage contrasts with the pressure facing CoreWeave and Nebius , whose borrowing costs and stock valuations have come under scrutiny.

Funds managed by BlackRock and Goldman Sachs Asset Management, alongside KKR-advised capital accounts, have also made anchor commitments. The transaction illustrates how AI infrastructure borrowing is evolving beyond conventional corporate loans and bonds. It also gives SpaceX access to additional hardware without requiring the entire purchase amount upfront, although the company still assumes substantial multiyear payment obligations. SpaceX is no longer primarily a rocket-launch and satellite-connectivity business. Its Super Intelligence division generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue, surpassing the $5.25 billion reported by its connectivity division, which includes Starlink. That AI revenue expansion helps explain the company's appetite for additional computing capacity. Management expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of $35 billion-$40 billion as investment in infrastructure accelerates. The company is also selling computing capacity to outside customers. An earlier Reflection AI agreement demonstrated how its Colossus facilities could generate revenue beyond supporting Grok models. The new hardware will use Nvidia's Vera Rubin architecture, extending a technology relationship already central to SpaceX's computing strategy . SpaceX executives claim some infrastructure investments can pay for themselves in less than one year. However, such expectations depend on utilization, operating costs and customers continuing to purchase computing capacity. The timing is particularly significant because financing conditions have deteriorated for specialized AI cloud providers. Musk recently warned that more than 200 neocloud companies could face widespread consolidation or failure as lenders become increasingly reluctant to finance businesses dependent almost entirely on AI infrastructure revenue. Unlike many smaller cloud providers, SpaceX benefits from established rocket-launch and Starlink operations. Musk argues that this diversified revenue supports its access to investment-grade financing. That advantage contrasts with the pressure facing CoreWeave and Nebius , whose borrowing costs and stock valuations have come under scrutiny. iPad owners (with the exception of iPad Pro owners, who are a whole different breed) tend not to worry too much about tech specs.

extraction.body: Apple has had a busy fall, with the launch of the iPhone Duo, HomeView smart hub, and the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. But there’s one more event this week, and it might be the biggest of all. And you can follow every rumor and announcement with us right here. Apple kicked off its week of releases with the new iPad mini , which got a thinner design, new A20 Pro chip, and an OLED display. As you can guess by the thinly veiled pun, this week’s marquee announcement is a new MacBook Pro, but not just any MacBook Pro. Here’s what else we’re expecting to see: Touchscreen MacBook Pro: After years of denials, Apple appears to be on the verge of releasing its first-ever touchscreen MacBook . Rumors say it will have a new design with a lighter chassis, Dynamic Island, and an OLED display. And a very high price tag. M6 iMac: Apple announced the M6 chip in the Mac mini last month and now it’ll reportedly make its way into the iMac . There could be new colors too. M6 MacBook Pro: The entry-level MacBook Pro gets its annual chip-and-ship upgrade. We’re still expecting three more announcements this week, the M6 iMac, the M6 entry-level MacBook Pro, and the touchscreen MacBook Pro. We assume tomorrow will bring the updates to the iMac and MacBook Pro and Wednesday will cap the announcements with the touchscreen model. It’s going to be a fun week! Over the past several years, Apple has put renewed emphasis on device thinness, with the M4 iPad Pro , iPhone Air , and iPhone Duo all competing for the crown of thinnest device. The iPad mini shaved off a considerable amount of thickness, going from 6.3mm to 5.4mm, but it’s still not quite as thin as other devices in Apple’s lineup: Apple is including a $9 Polishing Cloth with the iPad mini, but only if you spring for the nano display option, which costs $100 adn is only available on the 256GB and 512GB models. Still that’s a nice perk that iPhone Duo buyers sadly don’t get. Following the launch of the iPad mini this morning, Apple exec Greg Joswiak has teased a week of “exciting” announcements. That probably means we’re getting the M6 iMac and M6 MacBook Pro tomorrow and the touchscreen MacBook Pro on Wednesday. So stay tuned all week! While the iPad mini has all the makings of a pro device, with an OLED display, A20 Pro processor, and refined color palette, but it’s still missing one major feature of Apple’s other Pro devices: 120Hz ProMotion. There were scattered reports that Apple would be bringing the high-end screen tech to the mini along with its OLED upgrade, but alas, it didn’t make the cut. Looks like we’ll have to wait another 2-3 years. iPad owners (with the exception of iPad Pro owners, who are a whole different breed) tend not to worry too much about tech specs. For the majority of Apple’s customers the iPad is a convenient way to read their emails and browse the internet on the couch, and you don’t need the very latest chip to accomplish that. So it might seem odd, even gratuitous, that the new iPad mini has a processor (the A20 Pro) that’s three generations newer than the A17 Pro in the last model. But the key concept here is future-proofing. Because iPad owners have relatively low hardware requirements, they tend not to upgrade their devices very often. The iPad mini absolutely does not need to be this fast right now. But it will in five years, when the people who buy it this month will very likely still be using it. I mean, there’s also AI. That’s how Apple is officially marketing the A20 Pro. But I would argue that cutting-edge AI performance is a pretty low priority for most of the mini’s prospective customers. Since its 2021 redesign, the iPad mini has been available in multiple colors, including blue, purple, and pink. With the launch of the 8th-gen model, there are now just two: Midnight (black) and Starlight (gold). For a device that usually goes caseless, those are disapppointing options. And from what we see on the website, Midnight looks a lot closer to space gray than dark blue, but we’ll need to see it in person. Apple has hidden a pretty nice upgrade in the tech specs. The 128GB and 256GB version of the iPad mini have a cut-down A20 Pro processor with a 5-core CPU and a single 16-core Neural Engine. But if you opt for the 512GB model you get the full version of the chip, with a 6-core CPU and a dual 16-core Neural Engine. I don’t know if you need that much power in an iPad mini or want to spend $999 on a 8.5-inch tablet, but at least you’re getting a little more for your money. Apple has announced the new iPad mini with a slew of upgrades: An OLED display, thinner and lighter design, A20 Pro processor, and water and dust resistance. That’s a bunch of firsts for a non-Pro iPad and a massive upgrade. The screen is now 8.5 inches (up from 8.3 inches) and the camera is now on the landscape edge. It also got a price hike, but not as bad as feared: $699. Since Apple has only announced one day of announcements, one of three things could happen today: An iPad mini announcement at 9 am ET, 1 pm ET, or nothing at all. Mark Gurman thinks the mini could arrive today , though he frames it as a guess rather than his usual information from sources. So stick around, because something might be coming soon. All signs point to a new iPad mini arriving today. (Bear in mind, of course, that signs can be wrong.) Which raises an important question: Who cares? When it was first unveiled in 2012 the mini seemed like the tablet of the future. Attractive, portable, and capable, it had all the ingredients for success. But since then it’s been squeezed by developments at either end of the range. iPads have gained bigger screens and more powerful specs at the upper end, and are now suitable for work and entertainment in a way that the diminutive mini can’t match. On the other hand, why buy an iPad mini as well as a phone when you can get a big-screen iPhone such as the 18 Pro Max or Duo and have a capable device that can fulfil both functions? The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, very nearly as big as that of the original mini and not far behind its current 8.3 inches. And the Duo fits that screen into a far more pocketable chassis. The iPad mini doesn’t even have affordability to recommend it these days, starting at a scarcely budget-friendly $599. The cheap option is the standard iPad at $449, and that comes with a bigger display. Today’s challenge will be to make the iPad mini relevant again. An OLED screen is a nice idea, but is it enough to shift perceptions of a product that faces superior alternatives in every direction? What about an IP rating and a 2nm processor? My colleague Mahmoud Itani thinks the iPad mini is ready to become the best tablet for everyone , but it won’t be easy. The iPhone Duo and the HomeView home hub are both very cool and desirable products, but neither of them make a whole lot of sense. At least in the cold, logical, ‘essential tool for everyday life’ type of way. They’re products that everyone wants and nobody needs. This week could see Apple add a third entry to that list. Does a touchscreen MacBook make sense? Not really, as we discuss in this week’s Apple Breakfast column , but that doesn’t mean it will fail. When Apple released the iPad in 2010, Steve Jobs described why adding a touchscreen to one of Apple’s existing laptops wasn’t the right move: “We’ve done tons of user testing on this, and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives a great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off; it doesn’t work. It’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal, hence touchpads for a notebook. That’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.” How will Apple sell its new touchscreen Mac to the public? According to Mark Gurman , it will be billed as an “optional” feature rather than a primary one, not unlike the Touch Bar. And, well, we all know how that went . With several new Macs and one new iPad reportedly on the way, we could be in store for several days of announcements. Maybe the iPad mini on Monday, the M6 iMac and MacBook Pro on Tuesday, and the touchscreen MacBook on Wednesday? We’ll find out soon.

What about an IP rating and a 2nm processor? My colleague Mahmoud Itani thinks the iPad mini is ready to become the best tablet for everyone , but it won’t be easy.

The iPhone Duo and the HomeView home hub are both very cool and desirable products, but neither of them make a whole lot of sense. At least in the cold, logical, ‘essential tool for everyday life’ type of way. They’re products that everyone wants and nobody needs.
This week could see Apple add a third entry to that list. Does a touchscreen MacBook make sense? Not really, as we discuss in this week’s Apple Breakfast column , but that doesn’t mean it will fail.
When Apple released the iPad in 2010, Steve Jobs described why adding a touchscreen to one of Apple’s existing laptops wasn’t the right move:

“We’ve done tons of user testing on this, and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives a great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off; it doesn’t work. It’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal, hence touchpads for a notebook. That’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.”

How will Apple sell its new touchscreen Mac to the public? According to Mark Gurman , it will be billed as an “optional” feature rather than a primary one, not unlike the Touch Bar. And, well, we all know how that went .

With several new Macs and one new iPad reportedly on the way, we could be in store for several days of announcements. Maybe the iPad mini on Monday, the M6 iMac and MacBook Pro on Tuesday, and the touchscreen MacBook on Wednesday? We’ll find out soon.

extraction.body: Apple has had a busy fall, with the launch of the iPhone Duo, HomeView smart hub, and the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. But there’s one more event this week, and it might be the biggest of all. And you can follow every rumor and announcement with us right here. Apple kicked off its week of releases with the new iPad mini , which got a thinner design, new A20 Pro chip, and an OLED display. As you can guess by the thinly veiled pun, this week’s marquee announcement is a new MacBook Pro, but not just any MacBook Pro. Here’s what else we’re expecting to see: Touchscreen MacBook Pro: After years of denials, Apple appears to be on the verge of releasing its first-ever touchscreen MacBook . Rumors say it will have a new design with a lighter chassis, Dynamic Island, and an OLED display. And a very high price tag. M6 iMac: Apple announced the M6 chip in the Mac mini last month and now it’ll reportedly make its way into the iMac . There could be new colors too. M6 MacBook Pro: The entry-level MacBook Pro gets its annual chip-and-ship upgrade. We’re still expecting three more announcements this week, the M6 iMac, the M6 entry-level MacBook Pro, and the touchscreen MacBook Pro. We assume tomorrow will bring the updates to the iMac and MacBook Pro and Wednesday will cap the announcements with the touchscreen model. It’s going to be a fun week! Over the past several years, Apple has put renewed emphasis on device thinness, with the M4 iPad Pro , iPhone Air , and iPhone Duo all competing for the crown of thinnest device. The iPad mini shaved off a considerable amount of thickness, going from 6.3mm to 5.4mm, but it’s still not quite as thin as other devices in Apple’s lineup: Apple is including a $9 Polishing Cloth with the iPad mini, but only if you spring for the nano display option, which costs $100 adn is only available on the 256GB and 512GB models. Still that’s a nice perk that iPhone Duo buyers sadly don’t get. Following the launch of the iPad mini this morning, Apple exec Greg Joswiak has teased a week of “exciting” announcements. That probably means we’re getting the M6 iMac and M6 MacBook Pro tomorrow and the touchscreen MacBook Pro on Wednesday. So stay tuned all week! While the iPad mini has all the makings of a pro device, with an OLED display, A20 Pro processor, and refined color palette, but it’s still missing one major feature of Apple’s other Pro devices: 120Hz ProMotion. There were scattered reports that Apple would be bringing the high-end screen tech to the mini along with its OLED upgrade, but alas, it didn’t make the cut. Looks like we’ll have to wait another 2-3 years. iPad owners (with the exception of iPad Pro owners, who are a whole different breed) tend not to worry too much about tech specs. For the majority of Apple’s customers the iPad is a convenient way to read their emails and browse the internet on the couch, and you don’t need the very latest chip to accomplish that. So it might seem odd, even gratuitous, that the new iPad mini has a processor (the A20 Pro) that’s three generations newer than the A17 Pro in the last model. But the key concept here is future-proofing. Because iPad owners have relatively low hardware requirements, they tend not to upgrade their devices very often. The iPad mini absolutely does not need to be this fast right now. But it will in five years, when the people who buy it this month will very likely still be using it. I mean, there’s also AI. That’s how Apple is officially marketing the A20 Pro. But I would argue that cutting-edge AI performance is a pretty low priority for most of the mini’s prospective customers. Since its 2021 redesign, the iPad mini has been available in multiple colors, including blue, purple, and pink. With the launch of the 8th-gen model, there are now just two: Midnight (black) and Starlight (gold). For a device that usually goes caseless, those are disapppointing options. And from what we see on the website, Midnight looks a lot closer to space gray than dark blue, but we’ll need to see it in person. Apple has hidden a pretty nice upgrade in the tech specs. The 128GB and 256GB version of the iPad mini have a cut-down A20 Pro processor with a 5-core CPU and a single 16-core Neural Engine. But if you opt for the 512GB model you get the full version of the chip, with a 6-core CPU and a dual 16-core Neural Engine. I don’t know if you need that much power in an iPad mini or want to spend $999 on a 8.5-inch tablet, but at least you’re getting a little more for your money. Apple has announced the new iPad mini with a slew of upgrades: An OLED display, thinner and lighter design, A20 Pro processor, and water and dust resistance. That’s a bunch of firsts for a non-Pro iPad and a massive upgrade. The screen is now 8.5 inches (up from 8.3 inches) and the camera is now on the landscape edge. It also got a price hike, but not as bad as feared: $699. Since Apple has only announced one day of announcements, one of three things could happen today: An iPad mini announcement at 9 am ET, 1 pm ET, or nothing at all. Mark Gurman thinks the mini could arrive today , though he frames it as a guess rather than his usual information from sources. So stick around, because something might be coming soon. All signs point to a new iPad mini arriving today. (Bear in mind, of course, that signs can be wrong.) Which raises an important question: Who cares? When it was first unveiled in 2012 the mini seemed like the tablet of the future. Attractive, portable, and capable, it had all the ingredients for success. But since then it’s been squeezed by developments at either end of the range. iPads have gained bigger screens and more powerful specs at the upper end, and are now suitable for work and entertainment in a way that the diminutive mini can’t match. On the other hand, why buy an iPad mini as well as a phone when you can get a big-screen iPhone such as the 18 Pro Max or Duo and have a capable device that can fulfil both functions? The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, very nearly as big as that of the original mini and not far behind its current 8.3 inches. And the Duo fits that screen into a far more pocketable chassis. Apple kicked off its week of releases with the new iPad mini , which got a thinner design, new A20 Pro chip, and an OLED display. As you can guess by the thinly veiled pun, this week’s marquee announcement is a new MacBook Pro, but not just any MacBook Pro. Here’s what else we’re expecting to see:

Touchscreen MacBook Pro: After years of denials, Apple appears to be on the verge of releasing its first-ever touchscreen MacBook . Rumors say it will have a new design with a lighter chassis, Dynamic Island, and an OLED display. And a very high price tag.
M6 iMac: Apple announced the M6 chip in the Mac mini last month and now it’ll reportedly make its way into the iMac . There could be new colors too.
M6 MacBook Pro: The entry-level MacBook Pro gets its annual chip-and-ship upgrade.

We’re still expecting three more announcements this week, the M6 iMac, the M6 entry-level MacBook Pro, and the touchscreen MacBook Pro. We assume tomorrow will bring the updates to the iMac and MacBook Pro and Wednesday will cap the announcements with the touchscreen model. It’s going to be a fun week!

Over the past several years, Apple has put renewed emphasis on device thinness, with the M4 iPad Pro , iPhone Air , and iPhone Duo all competing for the crown of thinnest device. The iPad mini shaved off a considerable amount of thickness, going from 6.3mm to 5.4mm, but it’s still not quite as thin as other devices in Apple’s lineup:

Apple is including a $9 Polishing Cloth with the iPad mini, but only if you spring for the nano display option, which costs $100 adn is only available on the 256GB and 512GB models. Still that’s a nice perk that iPhone Duo buyers sadly don’t get.

Following the launch of the iPad mini this morning, Apple exec Greg Joswiak has teased a week of “exciting” announcements. That probably means we’re getting the M6 iMac and M6 MacBook Pro tomorrow and the touchscreen MacBook Pro on Wednesday. So stay tuned all week!

While the iPad mini has all the makings of a pro device, with an OLED display, A20 Pro processor, and refined color palette, but it’s still missing one major feature of Apple’s other Pro devices: 120Hz ProMotion. There were scattered reports that Apple would be bringing the high-end screen tech to the mini along with its OLED upgrade, but alas, it didn’t make the cut. Looks like we’ll have to wait another 2-3 years.

iPad owners (with the exception of iPad Pro owners, who are a whole different breed) tend not to worry too much about tech specs. For the majority of Apple’s customers the iPad is a convenient way to read their emails and browse the internet on the couch, and you don’t need the very latest chip to accomplish that. So it might seem odd, even gratuitous, that the new iPad mini has a processor (the A20 Pro) that’s three generations newer than the A17 Pro in the last model.

But the key concept here is future-proofing. Because iPad owners have relatively low hardware requirements, they tend not to upgrade their devices very often. The iPad mini absolutely does not need to be this fast right now. But it will in five years, when the people who buy it this month will very likely still be using it.

I mean, there’s also AI. That’s how Apple is officially marketing the A20 Pro. But I would argue that cutting-edge AI performance is a pretty low priority for most of the mini’s prospective customers.

Since its 2021 redesign, the iPad mini has been available in multiple colors, including blue, purple, and pink. With the launch of the 8th-gen model, there are now just two: Midnight (black) and Starlight (gold). For a device that usually goes caseless, those are disapppointing options. And from what we see on the website, Midnight looks a lot closer to space gray than dark blue, but we’ll need to see it in person.

sources.title: Apple Debuts $699 Water-Resistant iPad Mini With OLED Screen - Bloomberg.com
passages: Apple Inc. on Monday unveiled a revamped iPad mini with an OLED display, water-resistant design and faster chip, kicking off a week of product launches.
The tablet, priced at $699, features an 8.5-inch OLED, or organic light-emitting diode, screen that delivers deeper blacks, brighter whites and improved contrast.
Apple has increased the display size from the previous 8.3 inches by slimming down the bezels around the panel.

The redesigned device also includes a new “Acoustic Display” audio system that places the speakers beneath the display, helping to make this the first iPad with an IP67 dust and water resistance rating.

Apple on Oct 26 unveiled a revamped iPad mini with an OLED display, water-resistant design and faster chip, kicking off a week of product launches. The new tablet, priced at US$699 (S$895), features an 8.5-inch OLED, or organic light-emitting diode, screen that delivers deeper blacks, brighter whites and improved contrast. The redesigned device also includes a revamped audio system that places the speakers beneath the display, making it the first iPad with an IP67 water and dust-resistance rating. The new model also features the A20 Pro chip, an upgrade from the A17 Pro processor in the previous iPad mini, which started at US$599. It comes in both standard and nano-texture display options and storage configurations ranging from 128 gigabytes to half a terabyte. The latest iPad mini kicks off a series of late-October product introductions from Apple. Later this week, the company plans to unveil a new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip, before closing out the week with its first touch-screen MacBook Pro. Pre-orders for the new iPad mini begin on Oct 28 and it goes on sale on Nov 6. The new model comes in midnight and starlight colour options. A version with 512 gigabytes of storage and the matte display tops out at US$1,099. The cellular versions include Apple’s in-house C2 chip, a first for an iPad. extraction.body: Apple's iPads are popular tablets, and the brand offers several models. But while there are plenty of iPads to choose from, figuring out which ones are actually the newest isn't straightforward. Unlike Apple's iPhone lineup, iPads don't follow a simple numbering system, so model names alone don't tell you how new an iPad is. And that can be confusing since some stores may still carry older models. We'll walk you through the newest iPads, show you how to identify them, and explain what each one offers. Right now, the newest iPads are the M4-powered iPad Air models, which were released in March 2026. Apple's current lineup also includes the M5-powered iPad Pro, the standard iPad with an A16 chip, and the iPad Mini with an A17 Pro chip. Once you factor in different sizes, there are six iPads to choose from. Here's the current lineup, listed from the newest iPad to the oldest: Below, you'll find a complete breakdown of the latest iPads, including what makes each one worth considering and full pricing details. Editor's note: A new iPad Mini model is heavily rumored to debut at an upcoming Apple event on October 27 and 28. We'll add details for any new iPad models to this roundup once they're announced. Apple's latest iPad Air uses the company's M4 processor and boasts more memory, enabling better performance for creative tasks and AI tools. Apple refreshed its iPad Air lineup in March 2026 with new 11-inch and 13-inch models. This latest generation makes the jump from the brand's M3 chip to its newer M4, which Apple says delivers up to a 30% performance boost. Along with faster overall speeds, the upgraded chip should make a noticeable difference in gaming and creative work, while faster memory bandwidth is designed to better handle AI-driven tasks. The new iPad Air offers the same connectivity upgrades as the latest iPad Pro. That includes Apple's C1X modem for quicker cellular performance and the N1 wireless chip, which adds support for WiFi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. Beyond their new chip and connectivity options, the M4-powered iPad Airs carry over the same core design and feature set as their predecessors. Both sizes support the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the newer Apple Pencil Pro, which adds features such as a squeeze sensor and a gyroscope. Though the 2026 iPad Air originally launched at the same price as the previous generation, Apple has since increased its prices. The 11-inch model now starts at $749, up from $599, and the 13-inch starts at $949, up from $799. The 2026 11-inch iPad Air model numbers are A3459 for the WiFi-only edition and A3460 for the WiFi + Cellular option. Meanwhile, the model numbers for the latest 13-inch iPad Air are A3461 for the WiFi edition and A3462 for the WiFi + Cellular model. The new 2025 iPad Pro features Apple's latest-generation chip, the M5, which Apple says offers up to a 3.5x boost in AI performance compared to the last-generation iPad. It also offers a bump in graphical performance for 3D games and applications. Apple's latest high-end iPad Pro arrived in October 2025. Both the 11-inch and 13-inch iPad Pro models received a major under-the-hood upgrade. Instead of the M4 chip found in the 2024 models, these new Pros run on Apple's M5 processor. The M5 is the most powerful chip ever used in an iPad, built to deliver noticeable gains in AI and 3D performance over the M4. Apple has also improved memory bandwidth and storage, which should help with smoother multitasking and faster read and write performance. The 2025 iPad Pro models with cellular use Apple's C1X modem, which the company says can deliver up to a 50% boost in data performance compared to the M4 versions. Apple has also added its new N1 wireless chip, which supports WiFi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. On the outside, Apple didn't mess with a good thing. The new iPad Pros keep the ultra-thin design of their predecessors, measuring just 5.3mm for the 11-inch model and 5.1mm for the 13-inch model. Each model also sticks with Apple's Tandem OLED display, introduced on the previous-gen iPad Pros, which offers better contrast and sharper clarity than standard LED screens. The 2025 iPads are also compatible with Apple's Magic Keyboard, Apple Pencil (USB-C), Apple Pencil Pro, and Smart Folio.
