extraction.body: Apple confirmed on October 19, 2026 that it will hold a special event called “ Pro and tell ” on October 28, starting at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time in Los Angeles. The announcement itself is short on detail. Apple named the date, the time, the city, and the tagline, and left everything else to speculation, according to Engadget . That gap between what Apple said and what the rumor mill expects is the real story here, because the stakes riding on this single event are larger than a routine spec bump. Reports from multiple outlets point toward a touchscreen MacBook Pro , Apple’s first laptop with an OLED display, and a batch of related hardware. None of that is confirmed by Apple. This article separates what the company has actually said from what analysts and leakers are projecting onto an invite that, so far, contains four facts and a pun. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Strip away the speculation and the confirmed record is short. Apple sent media invitations for an event titled “Pro and tell,” set for October 28, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time, held in Los Angeles. That is the full extent of what the company has put in writing. Apple’s invitation does not name a single product, does not list a chip, and does not mention a price, according to CNBC . Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, added a public teaser of his own on social media. “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” he wrote, a line that confirms enthusiasm inside Apple’s marketing team without confirming any hardware. The post reads like classic pre-event misdirection: a nudge that keeps the story alive without giving reporters anything new to verify. That distinction between confirmed and rumored matters for anyone budgeting a laptop purchase around this date. Apple events built around wordplay tend to hint at the product category (a “tell” for the Pro line, echoing the “show” theme of prior launches), but the company has broken from its own pattern before, most recently when iPad announcements slipped into a Mac-focused showcase without warning. The single loudest rumor around October 28 is a touchscreen MacBook Pro, something Apple has resisted for over a decade while rivals built entire product lines around the feature. TechRadar frames the event as the possible arrival of exactly that laptop, pointing to years of patent filings and supply-chain leaks that all pointed the same direction. Apple executives have gone on record for years dismissing touchscreen Macs as ergonomically wrong, arguing that reaching up to poke a vertical display tires the arm faster than using a trackpad. That stance never fully squared with Apple’s own iPadOS roadmap, which has spent several cycles adding trackpad support, external keyboards, and windowing features that make an iPad behave more like a Mac. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would complete that convergence from the other direction. Reports also describe 14-inch and 16-inch model sizes carrying the feature, matching the sizes Apple has sold since the 2021 redesign. None of that is in Apple’s own announcement. The company’s invitation does not name a screen size, a chip, or a form factor, so every spec floating around right now sits in the “expected” column rather than the “confirmed” one. Our earlier coverage of the OLED MacBook Pro ship-date leak tracked this same rumor chain before Apple set a date for it. Apple has already made the OLED jump on iPhone, iPad Pro, and Apple Watch. The MacBook Pro remains one of the last major holdouts still shipping with a mini-LED panel, a technology Apple itself introduced to the line only a few years ago. Mini-LED delivers strong contrast and solid brightness, but it cannot match OLED for per-pixel black levels or the thinner module stack that OLED panels allow. Ten rows, three confirmed facts, seven open questions. That ratio is unusually lopsided even by Apple’s own secretive standards, and it explains why so much of the pre-event coverage reads like a hedge rather than a report. Apple’s event names rarely arrive by accident. “Pro and tell” riffs on the childhood classroom ritual of show and tell, swapping in the word that sits in nearly every product name on Apple’s Mac lineup: MacBook Pro, Mac Studio , iPad Pro. That wordplay points hard at the Pro tier of Apple’s lineup rather than a consumer refresh, which lines up with the MacBook Pro rumors dominating the coverage. It also signals scale. Apple reserves in-person Los Angeles events, rather than a prerecorded video posted to its newsroom, for launches the company wants treated as a moment rather than a routine spec refresh. The last redesign of this magnitude, the 2021 shift to M1 Pro and M1 Max chips, arrived with its own dedicated keynote rather than a press release buried in a product page update. That history matters for the chip story too. Our prior coverage of the M5 Pro and M5 Max fusion architecture already laid out the bandwidth gains Apple built into this chip generation. If October 28 is when those chips finally land in a MacBook Pro, the display story becomes secondary to a much bigger generational leap in Apple’s silicon roadmap. Apple’s last serious attempt at touch input on a MacBook Pro was the Touch Bar, a narrow OLED strip above the keyboard introduced in 2016. It replaced the function-key row with context-sensitive software buttons, and it never found a devoted fan base among professional users. Apple quietly dropped the feature from the lineup in 2021, swapping it back for physical function keys without much fanfare. That history is why longtime Mac users treat touchscreen rumors with some skepticism. Apple has tried a half-measure on touch input before and walked it back. A full touchscreen display would be a far bigger bet than a narrow OLED strip, and a far harder one to quietly discontinue if it does not land well with the people who buy MacBook Pro machines for work. The 2021 MacBook Pro redesign is the closest precedent for what an October 28 keynote might look like if the rumors hold up. That launch brought back MagSafe charging, restored an HDMI port and SD card slot after years of all-USB-C minimalism, and introduced the notch-equipped display alongside the first M1 Pro and M1 Max chips. It reversed several of Apple’s own prior design decisions in one keynote, something the company rarely does twice in a row. If Apple is willing to reverse course on touch input the way it reversed course on ports in 2021, October 28 would mark the most significant MacBook Pro redesign since that event. If the rumors turn out wrong, this becomes a far quieter chip refresh dressed up with a catchy event name. October 28 is not an isolated announcement. It is Apple’s second dedicated hardware event in a single month, following a smart-home showcase earlier in October that introduced Apple’s HomeView platform, covered in our report on Apple HomeView’s $299 launch . Stacking two major hardware events inside one month is unusual even for a company that typically spreads announcements across September, October, and a spring refresh cycle. A touchscreen Mac raises a software question Apple has avoided answering directly for over a decade: whether macOS itself gets touch-optimized controls, or whether a touchscreen simply layers on top of an interface designed for a cursor. Apple’s recent iPadOS updates have pushed in the opposite direction, adding desktop-style windowing and pointer support to what used to be a pure touch platform. A touchscreen Mac would close that gap from both sides at once, and developers who build for both platforms would need to think seriously about how their apps behave when a user’s finger, rather than a cursor, is the primary input. A confirmed touchscreen MacBook Pro would remove the single biggest marketing talking point Windows OEMs have used against Apple’s laptop lineup for a decade. Sales teams at Dell, HP, and Lenovo have leaned on “Mac doesn’t even do touch” as a differentiator in enterprise procurement conversations, and that line disappears the moment Apple ships the feature itself. It would also reshape the premium laptop price conversation. Apple’s MacBook Pro line already sits at the top of the market on price. Layering OLED and touch input onto that lineup gives Apple a case for holding, or even raising, prices at a moment when memory and component costs are already squeezing the entire PC industry, a trend our earlier report on the Apple Silicon threat facing Nvidia’s RTX Spark launch also touched on from the GPU side of the hardware market. Component suppliers stand to benefit regardless of how the keynote itself plays out. OLED panel makers, chip foundries, and case manufacturers tied to Apple’s supply chain all see demand spikes around a major MacBook Pro redesign, win or lose on the feature set Apple ultimately ships. Retail timing adds another layer to the story. An October 28 keynote lands just before the holiday shopping window opens in earnest, giving Apple roughly a month to get a redesigned MacBook Pro onto shelves before Black Friday. That schedule mirrors how Apple has handled iPhone launches for years, where a September announcement is built around maximizing holiday-quarter sales rather than simply clearing a backlog of finished engineering work. For resellers and retail partners, a redesign of this scale also means managing a transition period. Stores typically keep selling the outgoing MacBook Pro lineup at a discount for weeks after a new model is announced, which means shoppers who buy in the days immediately before October 28 could find themselves holding a device that drops in resale value the moment Apple’s keynote ends. Software teams building for the Mac have a narrower set of concerns than consumers chasing a shinier screen. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would force a fresh look at how existing macOS apps handle touch targets that were designed for a mouse pointer, where buttons and menu items are often too small or too close together for a fingertip. Enterprise IT departments managing large MacBook Pro fleets will also want clarity on whether a touch-capable model changes device management policies, accessory compatibility, or warranty terms before committing to a refresh cycle. Security teams have their own checklist too. Any new input method on an enterprise laptop expands the attack surface IT has to account for, and a touchscreen Mac would need its own guidance on lock-screen behavior, biometric pairing, and whether a stylus accessory introduces new pairing requirements for managed devices. Apple’s own marketing chief has already leaned into the hype, even without confirming specifics. Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, posted publicly ahead of the event: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” a post on social media that reads as a deliberate tease rather than a slip. It is the only on-record statement from an Apple executive tied directly to this event, and it confirms nothing beyond the fact that Apple’s marketing team is enjoying the wordplay as much as the press is. Tom’s Guide has tracked the rumor chain closely in the days since the invitation went out, framing the touchscreen question as the single detail most likely to define how the event is remembered regardless of what else Apple announces alongside it. Given how little Apple has confirmed in advance, the safest approach for anyone planning a purchase is to wait for the keynote itself rather than act on pre-event leaks. Rumors have been wrong about Apple hardware before, sometimes badly, and the gap between the three confirmed facts and the seven unconfirmed ones circulating right now is wide enough that real surprises are still possible. Reports mention M5 Pro, M5 Max, or M6 chips as possibilities, but none of these are confirmed by Apple as of this event announcement. Strip away the speculation and the confirmed record is short. Apple sent media invitations for an event titled “Pro and tell,” set for October 28, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time, held in Los Angeles. That is the full extent of what the company has put in writing. Apple’s invitation does not name a single product, does not list a chip, and does not mention a price, according to CNBC .

Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, added a public teaser of his own on social media. “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” he wrote, a line that confirms enthusiasm inside Apple’s marketing team without confirming any hardware. The post reads like classic pre-event misdirection: a nudge that keeps the story alive without giving reporters anything new to verify.

That distinction between confirmed and rumored matters for anyone budgeting a laptop purchase around this date. Apple events built around wordplay tend to hint at the product category (a “tell” for the Pro line, echoing the “show” theme of prior launches), but the company has broken from its own pattern before, most recently when iPad announcements slipped into a Mac-focused showcase without warning.

The single loudest rumor around October 28 is a touchscreen MacBook Pro, something Apple has resisted for over a decade while rivals built entire product lines around the feature. TechRadar frames the event as the possible arrival of exactly that laptop, pointing to years of patent filings and supply-chain leaks that all pointed the same direction.

Apple executives have gone on record for years dismissing touchscreen Macs as ergonomically wrong, arguing that reaching up to poke a vertical display tires the arm faster than using a trackpad. That stance never fully squared with Apple’s own iPadOS roadmap, which has spent several cycles adding trackpad support, external keyboards, and windowing features that make an iPad behave more like a Mac. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would complete that convergence from the other direction.

Reports also describe 14-inch and 16-inch model sizes carrying the feature, matching the sizes Apple has sold since the 2021 redesign. None of that is in Apple’s own announcement. The company’s invitation does not name a screen size, a chip, or a form factor, so every spec floating around right now sits in the “expected” column rather than the “confirmed” one. Our earlier coverage of the OLED MacBook Pro ship-date leak tracked this same rumor chain before Apple set a date for it.

Apple has already made the OLED jump on iPhone, iPad Pro, and Apple Watch. The MacBook Pro remains one of the last major holdouts still shipping with a mini-LED panel, a technology Apple itself introduced to the line only a few years ago. Mini-LED delivers strong contrast and solid brightness, but it cannot match OLED for per-pixel black levels or the thinner module stack that OLED panels allow.

Ten rows, three confirmed facts, seven open questions. That ratio is unusually lopsided even by Apple’s own secretive standards, and it explains why so much of the pre-event coverage reads like a hedge rather than a report.

Apple’s event names rarely arrive by accident. “Pro and tell” riffs on the childhood classroom ritual of show and tell, swapping in the word that sits in nearly every product name on Apple’s Mac lineup: MacBook Pro, Mac Studio , iPad Pro. That wordplay points hard at the Pro tier of Apple’s lineup rather than a consumer refresh, which lines up with the MacBook Pro rumors dominating the coverage.

It also signals scale. Apple reserves in-person Los Angeles events, rather than a prerecorded video posted to its newsroom, for launches the company wants treated as a moment rather than a routine spec refresh. The last redesign of this magnitude, the 2021 shift to M1 Pro and M1 Max chips, arrived with its own dedicated keynote rather than a press release buried in a product page update.

That history matters for the chip story too. Our prior coverage of the M5 Pro and M5 Max fusion architecture already laid out the bandwidth gains Apple built into this chip generation. If October 28 is when those chips finally land in a MacBook Pro, the display story becomes secondary to a much bigger generational leap in Apple’s silicon roadmap.

Apple’s last serious attempt at touch input on a MacBook Pro was the Touch Bar, a narrow OLED strip above the keyboard introduced in 2016. It replaced the function-key row with context-sensitive software buttons, and it never found a devoted fan base among professional users. Apple quietly dropped the feature from the lineup in 2021, swapping it back for physical function keys without much fanfare.

That history is why longtime Mac users treat touchscreen rumors with some skepticism. Apple has tried a half-measure on touch input before and walked it back. A full touchscreen display would be a far bigger bet than a narrow OLED strip, and a far harder one to quietly discontinue if it does not land well with the people who buy MacBook Pro machines for work.

The 2021 MacBook Pro redesign is the closest precedent for what an October 28 keynote might look like if the rumors hold up. That launch brought back MagSafe charging, restored an HDMI port and SD card slot after years of all-USB-C minimalism, and introduced the notch-equipped display alongside the first M1 Pro and M1 Max chips. It reversed several of Apple’s own prior design decisions in one keynote, something the company rarely does twice in a row.

If Apple is willing to reverse course on touch input the way it reversed course on ports in 2021, October 28 would mark the most significant MacBook Pro redesign since that event. If the rumors turn out wrong, this becomes a far quieter chip refresh dressed up with a catchy event name.

October 28 is not an isolated announcement. It is Apple’s second dedicated hardware event in a single month, following a smart-home showcase earlier in October that introduced Apple’s HomeView platform, covered in our report on Apple HomeView’s $299 launch . Stacking two major hardware events inside one month is unusual even for a company that typically spreads announcements across September, October, and a spring refresh cycle.

A touchscreen Mac raises a software question Apple has avoided answering directly for over a decade: whether macOS itself gets touch-optimized controls, or whether a touchscreen simply layers on top of an interface designed for a cursor. Apple’s recent iPadOS updates have pushed in the opposite direction, adding desktop-style windowing and pointer support to what used to be a pure touch platform. A touchscreen Mac would close that gap from both sides at once, and developers who build for both platforms would need to think seriously about how their apps behave when a user’s finger, rather than a cursor, is the primary input.

A confirmed touchscreen MacBook Pro would remove the single biggest marketing talking point Windows OEMs have used against Apple’s laptop lineup for a decade. Sales teams at Dell, HP, and Lenovo have leaned on “Mac doesn’t even do touch” as a differentiator in enterprise procurement conversations, and that line disappears the moment Apple ships the feature itself.

It would also reshape the premium laptop price conversation. Apple’s MacBook Pro line already sits at the top of the market on price. Layering OLED and touch input onto that lineup gives Apple a case for holding, or even raising, prices at a moment when memory and component costs are already squeezing the entire PC industry, a trend our earlier report on the Apple Silicon threat facing Nvidia’s RTX Spark launch also touched on from the GPU side of the hardware market.

Component suppliers stand to benefit regardless of how the keynote itself plays out. OLED panel makers, chip foundries, and case manufacturers tied to Apple’s supply chain all see demand spikes around a major MacBook Pro redesign, win or lose on the feature set Apple ultimately ships.

Retail timing adds another layer to the story. An October 28 keynote lands just before the holiday shopping window opens in earnest, giving Apple roughly a month to get a redesigned MacBook Pro onto shelves before Black Friday. That schedule mirrors how Apple has handled iPhone launches for years, where a September announcement is built around maximizing holiday-quarter sales rather than simply clearing a backlog of finished engineering work.

For resellers and retail partners, a redesign of this scale also means managing a transition period. Stores typically keep selling the outgoing MacBook Pro lineup at a discount for weeks after a new model is announced, which means shoppers who buy in the days immediately before October 28 could find themselves holding a device that drops in resale value the moment Apple’s keynote ends.

Software teams building for the Mac have a narrower set of concerns than consumers chasing a shinier screen. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would force a fresh look at how existing macOS apps handle touch targets that were designed for a mouse pointer, where buttons and menu items are often too small or too close together for a fingertip. Enterprise IT departments managing large MacBook Pro fleets will also want clarity on whether a touch-capable model changes device management policies, accessory compatibility, or warranty terms before committing to a refresh cycle.

Security teams have their own checklist too. Any new input method on an enterprise laptop expands the attack surface IT has to account for, and a touchscreen Mac would need its own guidance on lock-screen behavior, biometric pairing, and whether a stylus accessory introduces new pairing requirements for managed devices.

Apple’s own marketing chief has already leaned into the hype, even without confirming specifics. Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, posted publicly ahead of the event: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” a post on social media that reads as a deliberate tease rather than a slip. It is the only on-record statement from an Apple executive tied directly to this event, and it confirms nothing beyond the fact that Apple’s marketing team is enjoying the wordplay as much as the press is.

Tom’s Guide has tracked the rumor chain closely in the days since the invitation went out, framing the touchscreen question as the single detail most likely to define how the event is remembered regardless of what else Apple announces alongside it.

Given how little Apple has confirmed in advance, the safest approach for anyone planning a purchase is to wait for the keynote itself rather than act on pre-event leaks. Rumors have been wrong about Apple hardware before, sometimes badly, and the gap between the three confirmed facts and the seven unconfirmed ones circulating right now is wide enough that real surprises are still possible.

extraction.body: Apple confirmed on October 19, 2026 that it will hold a special event called “ Pro and tell ” on October 28, starting at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time in Los Angeles. The announcement itself is short on detail. Apple named the date, the time, the city, and the tagline, and left everything else to speculation, according to Engadget . That gap between what Apple said and what the rumor mill expects is the real story here, because the stakes riding on this single event are larger than a routine spec bump. Reports from multiple outlets point toward a touchscreen MacBook Pro , Apple’s first laptop with an OLED display, and a batch of related hardware. None of that is confirmed by Apple. This article separates what the company has actually said from what analysts and leakers are projecting onto an invite that, so far, contains four facts and a pun. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Strip away the speculation and the confirmed record is short. Apple sent media invitations for an event titled “Pro and tell,” set for October 28, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time, held in Los Angeles. That is the full extent of what the company has put in writing. Apple’s invitation does not name a single product, does not list a chip, and does not mention a price, according to CNBC . Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, added a public teaser of his own on social media. “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” he wrote, a line that confirms enthusiasm inside Apple’s marketing team without confirming any hardware. The post reads like classic pre-event misdirection: a nudge that keeps the story alive without giving reporters anything new to verify. That distinction between confirmed and rumored matters for anyone budgeting a laptop purchase around this date. Apple events built around wordplay tend to hint at the product category (a “tell” for the Pro line, echoing the “show” theme of prior launches), but the company has broken from its own pattern before, most recently when iPad announcements slipped into a Mac-focused showcase without warning. The single loudest rumor around October 28 is a touchscreen MacBook Pro, something Apple has resisted for over a decade while rivals built entire product lines around the feature. TechRadar frames the event as the possible arrival of exactly that laptop, pointing to years of patent filings and supply-chain leaks that all pointed the same direction. Apple executives have gone on record for years dismissing touchscreen Macs as ergonomically wrong, arguing that reaching up to poke a vertical display tires the arm faster than using a trackpad. That stance never fully squared with Apple’s own iPadOS roadmap, which has spent several cycles adding trackpad support, external keyboards, and windowing features that make an iPad behave more like a Mac. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would complete that convergence from the other direction. Reports also describe 14-inch and 16-inch model sizes carrying the feature, matching the sizes Apple has sold since the 2021 redesign. None of that is in Apple’s own announcement. The company’s invitation does not name a screen size, a chip, or a form factor, so every spec floating around right now sits in the “expected” column rather than the “confirmed” one. Our earlier coverage of the OLED MacBook Pro ship-date leak tracked this same rumor chain before Apple set a date for it. Apple has already made the OLED jump on iPhone, iPad Pro, and Apple Watch. The MacBook Pro remains one of the last major holdouts still shipping with a mini-LED panel, a technology Apple itself introduced to the line only a few years ago. Mini-LED delivers strong contrast and solid brightness, but it cannot match OLED for per-pixel black levels or the thinner module stack that OLED panels allow. Ten rows, three confirmed facts, seven open questions. That ratio is unusually lopsided even by Apple’s own secretive standards, and it explains why so much of the pre-event coverage reads like a hedge rather than a report. Apple’s event names rarely arrive by accident. “Pro and tell” riffs on the childhood classroom ritual of show and tell, swapping in the word that sits in nearly every product name on Apple’s Mac lineup: MacBook Pro, Mac Studio , iPad Pro. That wordplay points hard at the Pro tier of Apple’s lineup rather than a consumer refresh, which lines up with the MacBook Pro rumors dominating the coverage. It also signals scale. Apple reserves in-person Los Angeles events, rather than a prerecorded video posted to its newsroom, for launches the company wants treated as a moment rather than a routine spec refresh. The last redesign of this magnitude, the 2021 shift to M1 Pro and M1 Max chips, arrived with its own dedicated keynote rather than a press release buried in a product page update. That history matters for the chip story too. Our prior coverage of the M5 Pro and M5 Max fusion architecture already laid out the bandwidth gains Apple built into this chip generation. If October 28 is when those chips finally land in a MacBook Pro, the display story becomes secondary to a much bigger generational leap in Apple’s silicon roadmap. Apple’s last serious attempt at touch input on a MacBook Pro was the Touch Bar, a narrow OLED strip above the keyboard introduced in 2016. It replaced the function-key row with context-sensitive software buttons, and it never found a devoted fan base among professional users. Apple quietly dropped the feature from the lineup in 2021, swapping it back for physical function keys without much fanfare. That history is why longtime Mac users treat touchscreen rumors with some skepticism. Apple has tried a half-measure on touch input before and walked it back. A full touchscreen display would be a far bigger bet than a narrow OLED strip, and a far harder one to quietly discontinue if it does not land well with the people who buy MacBook Pro machines for work. The 2021 MacBook Pro redesign is the closest precedent for what an October 28 keynote might look like if the rumors hold up. That launch brought back MagSafe charging, restored an HDMI port and SD card slot after years of all-USB-C minimalism, and introduced the notch-equipped display alongside the first M1 Pro and M1 Max chips. It reversed several of Apple’s own prior design decisions in one keynote, something the company rarely does twice in a row. If Apple is willing to reverse course on touch input the way it reversed course on ports in 2021, October 28 would mark the most significant MacBook Pro redesign since that event. If the rumors turn out wrong, this becomes a far quieter chip refresh dressed up with a catchy event name. October 28 is not an isolated announcement. It is Apple’s second dedicated hardware event in a single month, following a smart-home showcase earlier in October that introduced Apple’s HomeView platform, covered in our report on Apple HomeView’s $299 launch . Stacking two major hardware events inside one month is unusual even for a company that typically spreads announcements across September, October, and a spring refresh cycle. A touchscreen Mac raises a software question Apple has avoided answering directly for over a decade: whether macOS itself gets touch-optimized controls, or whether a touchscreen simply layers on top of an interface designed for a cursor. Apple’s recent iPadOS updates have pushed in the opposite direction, adding desktop-style windowing and pointer support to what used to be a pure touch platform. A touchscreen Mac would close that gap from both sides at once, and developers who build for both platforms would need to think seriously about how their apps behave when a user’s finger, rather than a cursor, is the primary input. A confirmed touchscreen MacBook Pro would remove the single biggest marketing talking point Windows OEMs have used against Apple’s laptop lineup for a decade. Sales teams at Dell, HP, and Lenovo have leaned on “Mac doesn’t even do touch” as a differentiator in enterprise procurement conversations, and that line disappears the moment Apple ships the feature itself. It would also reshape the premium laptop price conversation. Apple’s MacBook Pro line already sits at the top of the market on price. Layering OLED and touch input onto that lineup gives Apple a case for holding, or even raising, prices at a moment when memory and component costs are already squeezing the entire PC industry, a trend our earlier report on the Apple Silicon threat facing Nvidia’s RTX Spark launch also touched on from the GPU side of the hardware market. Component suppliers stand to benefit regardless of how the keynote itself plays out. OLED panel makers, chip foundries, and case manufacturers tied to Apple’s supply chain all see demand spikes around a major MacBook Pro redesign, win or lose on the feature set Apple ultimately ships. Retail timing adds another layer to the story. An October 28 keynote lands just before the holiday shopping window opens in earnest, giving Apple roughly a month to get a redesigned MacBook Pro onto shelves before Black Friday. That schedule mirrors how Apple has handled iPhone launches for years, where a September announcement is built around maximizing holiday-quarter sales rather than simply clearing a backlog of finished engineering work. For resellers and retail partners, a redesign of this scale also means managing a transition period. Stores typically keep selling the outgoing MacBook Pro lineup at a discount for weeks after a new model is announced, which means shoppers who buy in the days immediately before October 28 could find themselves holding a device that drops in resale value the moment Apple’s keynote ends. Software teams building for the Mac have a narrower set of concerns than consumers chasing a shinier screen. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would force a fresh look at how existing macOS apps handle touch targets that were designed for a mouse pointer, where buttons and menu items are often too small or too close together for a fingertip. Strip away the speculation and the confirmed record is short. That is the full extent of what the company has put in writing. Apple’s invitation does not name a single product, does not list a chip, and does not mention a price, according to CNBC .

Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, added a public teaser of his own on social media. “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” he wrote, a line that confirms enthusiasm inside Apple’s marketing team without confirming any hardware. The post reads like classic pre-event misdirection: a nudge that keeps the story alive without giving reporters anything new to verify.

That distinction between confirmed and rumored matters for anyone budgeting a laptop purchase around this date. Apple events built around wordplay tend to hint at the product category (a “tell” for the Pro line, echoing the “show” theme of prior launches), but the company has broken from its own pattern before, most recently when iPad announcements slipped into a Mac-focused showcase without warning.

The single loudest rumor around October 28 is a touchscreen MacBook Pro, something Apple has resisted for over a decade while rivals built entire product lines around the feature. TechRadar frames the event as the possible arrival of exactly that laptop, pointing to years of patent filings and supply-chain leaks that all pointed the same direction.

Apple executives have gone on record for years dismissing touchscreen Macs as ergonomically wrong, arguing that reaching up to poke a vertical display tires the arm faster than using a trackpad. That stance never fully squared with Apple’s own iPadOS roadmap, which has spent several cycles adding trackpad support, external keyboards, and windowing features that make an iPad behave more like a Mac. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would complete that convergence from the other direction.

Reports also describe 14-inch and 16-inch model sizes carrying the feature, matching the sizes Apple has sold since the 2021 redesign. None of that is in Apple’s own announcement. The company’s invitation does not name a screen size, a chip, or a form factor, so every spec floating around right now sits in the “expected” column rather than the “confirmed” one. Our earlier coverage of the OLED MacBook Pro ship-date leak tracked this same rumor chain before Apple set a date for it.

Apple has already made the OLED jump on iPhone, iPad Pro, and Apple Watch. The MacBook Pro remains one of the last major holdouts still shipping with a mini-LED panel, a technology Apple itself introduced to the line only a few years ago. Mini-LED delivers strong contrast and solid brightness, but it cannot match OLED for per-pixel black levels or the thinner module stack that OLED panels allow.

Ten rows, three confirmed facts, seven open questions. That ratio is unusually lopsided even by Apple’s own secretive standards, and it explains why so much of the pre-event coverage reads like a hedge rather than a report.

Apple’s event names rarely arrive by accident. “Pro and tell” riffs on the childhood classroom ritual of show and tell, swapping in the word that sits in nearly every product name on Apple’s Mac lineup: MacBook Pro, Mac Studio , iPad Pro. That wordplay points hard at the Pro tier of Apple’s lineup rather than a consumer refresh, which lines up with the MacBook Pro rumors dominating the coverage.

It also signals scale. Apple reserves in-person Los Angeles events, rather than a prerecorded video posted to its newsroom, for launches the company wants treated as a moment rather than a routine spec refresh. The last redesign of this magnitude, the 2021 shift to M1 Pro and M1 Max chips, arrived with its own dedicated keynote rather than a press release buried in a product page update.

If October 28 is when those chips finally land in a MacBook Pro, the display story becomes secondary to a much bigger generational leap in Apple’s silicon roadmap.

Apple’s last serious attempt at touch input on a MacBook Pro was the Touch Bar, a narrow OLED strip above the keyboard introduced in 2016. It replaced the function-key row with context-sensitive software buttons, and it never found a devoted fan base among professional users. Apple quietly dropped the feature from the lineup in 2021, swapping it back for physical function keys without much fanfare.

That history is why longtime Mac users treat touchscreen rumors with some skepticism. Apple has tried a half-measure on touch input before and walked it back. A full touchscreen display would be a far bigger bet than a narrow OLED strip, and a far harder one to quietly discontinue if it does not land well with the people who buy MacBook Pro machines for work.

Sales teams at Dell, HP, and Lenovo have leaned on “Mac doesn’t even do touch” as a differentiator in enterprise procurement conversations, and that line disappears the moment Apple ships the feature itself.

extraction.body: Apple gives iPad mini its biggest update ever Featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance, faster wireless connectivity, and water and dust resistance CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today unveiled the all-new iPad mini , featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance. 1 The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience. 2 A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support. 3 With its incredible set of advanced features, it’s the most capable and versatile iPad mini ever. The new iPad mini is powered by iPadOS 27 with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions on virtually any topic with broad world knowledge, and understand what’s on their screen. 4 The combination of powerful features and game-changing iPadOS 27 capabilities makes the new iPad mini a compelling value. Customers can pre-order it along with the new Smart Folio starting Wednesday, October 28, with availability beginning Friday, November 6. “iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers,” said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.” At 5.4 mm thin, the new iPad mini is more portable than ever, and is available in two gorgeous finishes: a new midnight and a beautiful starlight. Remarkably thinner and lighter than the previous generation, iPad mini is now even easier to carry, whether a user is reading, working on the go, or using it with one hand. It also features an IP67 rating to protect against water and dust — ideal for a range of use cases, such as working outside on a rainy day or reading by the pool. 1 The new iPad mini comes with a stunning OLED display that delivers amazing front-of-screen performance and an even larger 8.5-inch size while maintaining the same footprint as the previous mini, thanks to 24 percent thinner bezels. 2 The Super Retina XDR display features OLED technology to deliver pixel-level lighting control for much deeper blacks and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vivid and accurate imagery. For an even better visual experience across a range of lighting conditions, iPad mini also features peak brightness of up to 1200 nits — more than 2x higher than the previous generation — and supports 600 nits of full-screen brightness for SDR and HDR content, along with a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. And with a 1-nit minimum brightness, iPad mini is even more suitable for dim environments, from users reading in bed at night to pilots checking their electronic flight bag in the cockpit. iPad mini also offers a new nano-texture display option, which users love on iPad Pro, that reduces glare in bright environments — ideal for creatives editing outdoors or technicians working in the field. Together, these display advancements extend the versatility of iPad mini across an even wider range of use cases. A20 Pro delivers a giant leap in performance for iPad mini, significantly boosting graphics and AI-intensive tasks. It is built using Apple’s latest 2-nanometer process technology and a new package inspired by M-series chips. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core, iPad mini delivers up to 4.5x faster AI performance than the previous generation — perfect for AI tasks ranging from running on-device models in creative apps to running local LLMs. 3 And with the latest graphics architecture, including dynamic caching and hardware-accelerated mesh shading and ray tracing, graphics performance jumps by up to 2.7x — great for gaming and 3D rendering. 3 A20 Pro also features up to a 6-core CPU for up to 60 percent faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks like editing photos and working across apps. 3 The 512GB configuration features a powerful Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which offers double the processing power of the previous generation, accelerating tasks in apps like Draw Things and Detail. By engaging all 32 cores, A20 Pro becomes a powerhouse for more advanced on-device AI workloads. A20 Pro also brings over a 2x increase in unified memory bandwidth, unlocking additional performance for new levels of capability and responsiveness across graphics and AI-intensive workloads. A Rich New Audio Experience and Advanced Cameras The new iPad mini features an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers are paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume. In addition, custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs. The Acoustic Display also features a sealed enclosure that helps iPad mini achieve its IP67 rating. The 12MP Center Stage front camera is now on the landscape edge, perfect for FaceTime calls, video conferencing, and collaboration. And the 12MP Wide back camera captures gorgeous photos with Smart HDR 4 and 4K video at up to 60 fps, while the addition of an Adaptive True Tone flash improves photos and makes document scanning better than ever. iPad mini now features N1, an Apple-designed wireless networking chip that enables Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. 5 N1 brings better performance when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the overall performance and reliability of features like AirDrop and AirPlay. 6 Cellular models of the new iPad mini feature C2, Apple’s next-generation cellular modem system. C2 enables up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds compared to the previous generation of iPad mini, with even greater power efficiency. 6 And with iPadOS 27, moving between cellular and Wi-Fi networks is more seamless than ever, so users can stay connected on a FaceTime call even while they’re in transit. Users can also enjoy the benefits of eSIM, which lets them quickly and securely add a new plan, connect and transfer existing plans digitally, and stay in touch with family and friends regardless of Wi-Fi availability. 7 iPadOS 27 with the Next Generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI iPad mini users can get even more done with Siri AI, rolling out in beta with iPadOS 27. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri, powered by Apple Intelligence, that is profoundly more personal, capable, and conversational. 4 iPad mini also supports Apple’s most advanced on-device model ever, for even more expressive voices with Siri AI as well as a major boost in accuracy with systemwide dictation. Siri AI can draw on personal context understanding to help users find what they need in the moment across their personal messages, emails, photos, and more; use onscreen awareness to take action related to the content on a user’s screen; and answer questions about virtually any topic. Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. Users can improve a photo’s composition after it’s been taken using tools such as upgraded Clean Up, Spatial Reframing, and Extend. And now the all-new Image Playground app offers photorealistic imagery. In Safari, Notify Me helps users monitor web pages for changes, like product restocks or price drops, and stay on top of updates. Apple Intelligence uses on-device processing and Private Cloud Compute to help protect users’ privacy. When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else. iPadOS 27 also delivers an expansive set of improvements that make iPad more responsive, reliable, and easy to use, along with updates to Liquid Glass, including a new slider in Settings that gives users the option to personalize it, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference. With iPadOS 27.2, iPad mini also supports extended display mode when connected to an external display, great for users multitasking with windowed apps. Additionally, powerful and easy-to-use tools help parents manage what their kids can see, who they can talk to, and when they have access to apps. For parents and families looking for more information on how to help create safer, more enriching digital experiences for their kids, Apple also has a website with details on the latest tools and how to get started using them. Accessories That Unlock More Ways to Be Productive and Creative The new Smart Folio features a two-panel architecture, offering a slim, lightweight cover that magnetically attaches to iPad mini. 8 Crafted with TechWoven fabric in navy blue and taupe to complement the iPad mini finishes, the Smart Folio has an adjustable design that gives users a greater range of motion, including new viewing angles, for enhanced versatility. iPad mini supports both Apple Pencil (USB-C) and Apple Pencil Pro, giving users two incredible options to bring their ideas to life. 8 Apple Pencil (USB-C) is a great value for everyday tasks like note-taking and sketching, while Apple Pencil Pro delivers industry-leading capabilities for the ultimate pencil experience. With Apple Pencil Pro, users can take advantage of innovative features like squeeze and barrel roll to work in entirely new ways, as well as utilize Find My support to help locate it when misplaced. iPad mini was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 35 percent recycled content overall, 9 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure and 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery. iPad mini is manufactured with 40 percent renewable energy, like wind and solar, across the supply chain. It is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. passages: Apple gives iPad mini its biggest update ever
Featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance, faster wireless connectivity, and water and dust resistance

CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today unveiled the all-new iPad mini , featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance. 1 The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience. 2 A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support. 3 With its incredible set of advanced features, it’s the most capable and versatile iPad mini ever.

The new iPad mini is powered by iPadOS 27 with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions on virtually any topic with broad world knowledge, and understand what’s on their screen. 4 The combination of powerful features and game-changing iPadOS 27 capabilities makes the new iPad mini a compelling value. Customers can pre-order it along with the new Smart Folio starting Wednesday, October 28, with availability beginning Friday, November 6.

“iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers,” said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.”

At 5.4 mm thin, the new iPad mini is more portable than ever, and is available in two gorgeous finishes: a new midnight and a beautiful starlight. Remarkably thinner and lighter than the previous generation, iPad mini is now even easier to carry, whether a user is reading, working on the go, or using it with one hand. It also features an IP67 rating to protect against water and dust — ideal for a range of use cases, such as working outside on a rainy day or reading by the pool. 1

The new iPad mini comes with a stunning OLED display that delivers amazing front-of-screen performance and an even larger 8.5-inch size while maintaining the same footprint as the previous mini, thanks to 24 percent thinner bezels. 2 The Super Retina XDR display features OLED technology to deliver pixel-level lighting control for much deeper blacks and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vivid and accurate imagery.

For an even better visual experience across a range of lighting conditions, iPad mini also features peak brightness of up to 1200 nits — more than 2x higher than the previous generation — and supports 600 nits of full-screen brightness for SDR and HDR content, along with a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. And with a 1-nit minimum brightness, iPad mini is even more suitable for dim environments, from users reading in bed at night to pilots checking their electronic flight bag in the cockpit. iPad mini also offers a new nano-texture display option, which users love on iPad Pro, that reduces glare in bright environments — ideal for creatives editing outdoors or technicians working in the field. Together, these display advancements extend the versatility of iPad mini across an even wider range of use cases.

A20 Pro delivers a giant leap in performance for iPad mini, significantly boosting graphics and AI-intensive tasks. It is built using Apple’s latest 2-nanometer process technology and a new package inspired by M-series chips. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core, iPad mini delivers up to 4.5x faster AI performance than the previous generation — perfect for AI tasks ranging from running on-device models in creative apps to running local LLMs. 3 And with the latest graphics architecture, including dynamic caching and hardware-accelerated mesh shading and ray tracing, graphics performance jumps by up to 2.7x — great for gaming and 3D rendering. 3 A20 Pro also features up to a 6-core CPU for up to 60 percent faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks like editing photos and working across apps. 3

The 512GB configuration features a powerful Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which offers double the processing power of the previous generation, accelerating tasks in apps like Draw Things and Detail. By engaging all 32 cores, A20 Pro becomes a powerhouse for more advanced on-device AI workloads. A20 Pro also brings over a 2x increase in unified memory bandwidth, unlocking additional performance for new levels of capability and responsiveness across graphics and AI-intensive workloads.
A Rich New Audio Experience and Advanced Cameras

The new iPad mini features an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers are paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume. In addition, custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs. The Acoustic Display also features a sealed enclosure that helps iPad mini achieve its IP67 rating.

The 12MP Center Stage front camera is now on the landscape edge, perfect for FaceTime calls, video conferencing, and collaboration. And the 12MP Wide back camera captures gorgeous photos with Smart HDR 4 and 4K video at up to 60 fps, while the addition of an Adaptive True Tone flash improves photos and makes document scanning better than ever.

iPad mini now features N1, an Apple-designed wireless networking chip that enables Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. 5 N1 brings better performance when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the overall performance and reliability of features like AirDrop and AirPlay. 6

Cellular models of the new iPad mini feature C2, Apple’s next-generation cellular modem system. C2 enables up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds compared to the previous generation of iPad mini, with even greater power efficiency. 6 And with iPadOS 27, moving between cellular and Wi-Fi networks is more seamless than ever, so users can stay connected on a FaceTime call even while they’re in transit. Users can also enjoy the benefits of eSIM, which lets them quickly and securely add a new plan, connect and transfer existing plans digitally, and stay in touch with family and friends regardless of Wi-Fi availability. 7
iPadOS 27 with the Next Generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI

iPad mini users can get even more done with Siri AI, rolling out in beta with iPadOS 27. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri, powered by Apple Intelligence, that is profoundly more personal, capable, and conversational. 4 iPad mini also supports Apple’s most advanced on-device model ever, for even more expressive voices with Siri AI as well as a major boost in accuracy with systemwide dictation.

Siri AI can draw on personal context understanding to help users find what they need in the moment across their personal messages, emails, photos, and more; use onscreen awareness to take action related to the content on a user’s screen; and answer questions about virtually any topic. Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. Users can improve a photo’s composition after it’s been taken using tools such as upgraded Clean Up, Spatial Reframing, and Extend. And now the all-new Image Playground app offers photorealistic imagery. In Safari, Notify Me helps users monitor web pages for changes, like product restocks or price drops, and stay on top of updates. Apple Intelligence uses on-device processing and Private Cloud Compute to help protect users’ privacy. When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else.

iPadOS 27 also delivers an expansive set of improvements that make iPad more responsive, reliable, and easy to use, along with updates to Liquid Glass, including a new slider in Settings that gives users the option to personalize it, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference. With iPadOS 27.2, iPad mini also supports extended display mode when connected to an external display, great for users multitasking with windowed apps.

Additionally, powerful and easy-to-use tools help parents manage what their kids can see, who they can talk to, and when they have access to apps. For parents and families looking for more information on how to help create safer, more enriching digital experiences for their kids, Apple also has a website with details on the latest tools and how to get started using them.
Accessories That Unlock More Ways to Be Productive and Creative

The new Smart Folio features a two-panel architecture, offering a slim, lightweight cover that magnetically attaches to iPad mini. 8 Crafted with TechWoven fabric in navy blue and taupe to complement the iPad mini finishes, the Smart Folio has an adjustable design that gives users a greater range of motion, including new viewing angles, for enhanced versatility.

iPad mini supports both Apple Pencil (USB-C) and Apple Pencil Pro, giving users two incredible options to bring their ideas to life. 8 Apple Pencil (USB-C) is a great value for everyday tasks like note-taking and sketching, while Apple Pencil Pro delivers industry-leading capabilities for the ultimate pencil experience. With Apple Pencil Pro, users can take advantage of innovative features like squeeze and barrel roll to work in entirely new ways, as well as utilize Find My support to help locate it when misplaced.

iPad mini was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 35 percent recycled content overall, 9 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure and 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery. iPad mini is manufactured with 40 percent renewable energy, like wind and solar, across the supply chain. It is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled.

Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.

The new iPad mini features the A20 Pro chip and the Super Retina XDR display that customers have come to appreciate for all the benefits the OLED displays have to offer. Here are all the new features that this iPad mini brings. Measuring at 5.4 mm thin, this is the thinnest iPad mini that Apple has ever designed. In fact, it’s just as thin as the current iPad Pro. The iPad mini comes in two gorgeous finishes: midnight and starlight. But the biggest improvement in the design has to be that the new iPad mini is now water- and dust-resistant with an IP67 rating, so you could safely use this iPad mini on a rainy day or by the pool. As mentioned before, the new iPad mini features a stunning Super Retina XDR display that’s also larger at 8.5 inches, yet it retains the same footprint as before. This means thinner bezels, so you can see more of your content. The Super Retina XDR display continues to bring the same benefits that Apple displays have been known for, including P3 wide color gamut and True Tone technology. This display also brings so many improvements across the board: For the 256GB and 512GB storage tiers, there is also a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare. It should be worth noting that the new iPad mini’s display seems to lack 120Hz ProMotion technology, so for those who were hoping to see that on the iPad mini, they’d be disappointed by this. The new iPad mini features the latest and greatest A20 chip – the same chip that’s found in both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo, and it’s the first A-series chip that’s built on the 2nm process. This translates to up to 60% faster multithreaded performance, up to 2.7x faster graphics performance, and up to 4.5x faster AI performance compared to the previous generation. Both the 128GB and the 256GB storage tiers feature a binned A20 Pro chip with 5 CPU cores (2 super / 3 efficient) and a single 16-core Neural Engine, but when you opt for the 512GB storage tier, you’ll get the full-fledged A20 Pro chip that includes the Dual 16-core Neural Engine. With that great amount of performance, it is even more capable of running the new Siri AI along with other latest features that iPadOS 27 has to offer. This water-resistant design is only made possible with the improvements Apple made to the speakers, and Apple has come up with an innovative solution called the “Acoustic Display”, which translates to two front-facing speakers that allow for an even more immersive audio experience for entertainment, gaming, and editing purposes. The 12MP Center Stage camera now moves to the landscape edge, which is now ideal for video calls, and the iPad mini continues to feature the 12MP Wide back camera with Smart HDR 4 and Adaptive True Tone flash for convenient scanning. Following suit with other recent Apple products, the new iPad mini features the N1 wireless networking chip that consolidates Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread for the most up-to-date wireless connectivity. The N1 also performs more optimally when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the reliability of peer-to-peer features like AirPlay and AirDrop. The C2 cellular modem, which made its debut on the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo, also made its way to the cellular models of the new iPad mini, bringing up to 50% faster cellular data speeds over the previous generation. The new Smart Folio for this iPad mini is now redesigned with a two-panel architecture, and it’s crafted with a TechWoven fabric. Offered in both navy blue and taupe, this Smart Folio continues to bring great protection to the iPad mini while featuring a lightweight design that props up your iPad mini at different angles, perfect for watching your favorite content. The new iPad mini continues to support both the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro as well. The new iPad mini starts at $699, which is a $100 price increase over the previous generation, but considering all the improvements, especially that OLED display, it could’ve been more expensive as previously predicted. The new iPad mini is offered in these storage configurations (prices shown for the Wi-Fi model): The nano-texture option (for the 256GB and 512GB storage tiers) is available as a $100 upgrade, and cellular connectivity is available as a $150 upgrade. Pre-orders start this Wednesday (October 28) at 10:10 a.m. PT, and they’ll arrive in stores and to customers starting November 6. Both the 128GB and the 256GB storage tiers feature a binned A20 Pro chip with 5 CPU cores (2 super / 3 efficient) and a single 16-core Neural Engine, but when you opt for the 512GB storage tier, you’ll get the full-fledged A20 Pro chip that includes the Dual 16-core Neural Engine. With that great amount of performance, it is even more capable of running the new Siri AI along with other latest features that iPadOS 27 has to offer.

This water-resistant design is only made possible with the improvements Apple made to the speakers, and Apple has come up with an innovative solution called the “Acoustic Display”, which translates to two front-facing speakers that allow for an even more immersive audio experience for entertainment, gaming, and editing purposes. The 12MP Center Stage camera now moves to the landscape edge, which is now ideal for video calls, and the iPad mini continues to feature the 12MP Wide back camera with Smart HDR 4 and Adaptive True Tone flash for convenient scanning.

Following suit with other recent Apple products, the new iPad mini features the N1 wireless networking chip that consolidates Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread for the most up-to-date wireless connectivity. The N1 also performs more optimally when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the reliability of peer-to-peer features like AirPlay and AirDrop.

The C2 cellular modem, which made its debut on the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo, also made its way to the cellular models of the new iPad mini, bringing up to 50% faster cellular data speeds over the previous generation.

The new Smart Folio for this iPad mini is now redesigned with a two-panel architecture, and it’s crafted with a TechWoven fabric. Offered in both navy blue and taupe, this Smart Folio continues to bring great protection to the iPad mini while featuring a lightweight design that props up your iPad mini at different angles, perfect for watching your favorite content.
The new iPad mini continues to support both the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro as well.

The new iPad mini starts at $699, which is a $100 price increase over the previous generation, but considering all the improvements, especially that OLED display, it could’ve been more expensive as previously predicted. The nano-texture option (for the 256GB and 512GB storage tiers) is available as a $100 upgrade, and cellular connectivity is available as a $150 upgrade.
Pre-orders start this Wednesday (October 28) at 10:10 a.m. PT, and they’ll arrive in stores and to customers starting November 6.

The new iPad mini also measures just 5.4mm thin, making it the most portable version of the device yet; on the processing side, the iPad mini now comes with the A20 Pro chip, carried straight from the iPhone 18 Pro – so you get all the latest and greatest Apple has to offer this year in a slightly bigger format. The 512GB configuration also features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine with double the AI processing power of the previous generation.

Despite housing a larger 8.5-inch screen, the overall footprint remains the same as the previous generation, thanks to bezels that are 24% thinner. The Super Retina XDR OLED display brings deeper blacks and supports the Apple P3 wide color gamut, with peak brightness reaching up to 1,200 nits (more than twice that of the previous generation, Apple says), while full-screen brightness for SDR and HDR content sits at 600 nits. A nano-texture display option is also available.

Audio has also been reworked through an Acoustic Display system, similar to Sony’s BRAVIA TVs which uses the entire panel to improve audio quality. Woofers are paired through the display for punchier bass, while custom tweeters are tucked between the glass and aluminum enclosure for cleaner high frequencies. Since this design does away with speaker grilles, Apple claims this is one of the ways the tablet achieved its IP67 ingress protection rating.

Apple has also relocated the 12MP Center Stage front camera to the landscape edge for more natural video call framing, while the rear 12MP wide camera supports Smart HDR 4 and 4K video at up to 60 fps, alongside a new Adaptive True Tone flash. Connectivity receives a significant upgrade with the N1 wireless networking chip, enabling Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread support; cellular models gain the C2 modem, which Apple says delivers up to 50% faster cellular data speeds than before, with improved power efficiency (plus there’s eSIM support as well).

Pre-orders for the new iPad mini open on 29 October 2026 via apple.com/my and the Apple Store app; units will begin arriving to customers and appear in Apple Store locations and Apple Authorised Resellers from 6 November 2026. The tablet is available in 128GB, 256GB, and 512GB configurations in Midnight and Starlight finishes. The Wi-Fi model starts at RM2,999 , while the Wi-Fi + Cellular model starts at RM3,699 .

extraction.body: Apple unleashed its biggest update to its smallest iPad ever! The new iPad mini features the A20 Pro chip and the Super Retina XDR display that customers have come to appreciate for all the benefits the OLED displays have to offer. Here are all the new features that this iPad mini brings. Measuring at 5.4 mm thin, this is the thinnest iPad mini that Apple has ever designed. In fact, it’s just as thin as the current iPad Pro. The iPad mini comes in two gorgeous finishes: midnight and starlight. But the biggest improvement in the design has to be that the new iPad mini is now water- and dust-resistant with an IP67 rating, so you could safely use this iPad mini on a rainy day or by the pool. As mentioned before, the new iPad mini features a stunning Super Retina XDR display that’s also larger at 8.5 inches, yet it retains the same footprint as before. This means thinner bezels, so you can see more of your content. The Super Retina XDR display continues to bring the same benefits that Apple displays have been known for, including P3 wide color gamut and True Tone technology. This display also brings so many improvements across the board: For the 256GB and 512GB storage tiers, there is also a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare. It should be worth noting that the new iPad mini’s display seems to lack 120Hz ProMotion technology, so for those who were hoping to see that on the iPad mini, they’d be disappointed by this. The new iPad mini features the latest and greatest A20 chip – the same chip that’s found in both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo, and it’s the first A-series chip that’s built on the 2nm process. This translates to up to 60% faster multithreaded performance, up to 2.7x faster graphics performance, and up to 4.5x faster AI performance compared to the previous generation. Both the 128GB and the 256GB storage tiers feature a binned A20 Pro chip with 5 CPU cores (2 super / 3 efficient) and a single 16-core Neural Engine, but when you opt for the 512GB storage tier, you’ll get the full-fledged A20 Pro chip that includes the Dual 16-core Neural Engine. With that great amount of performance, it is even more capable of running the new Siri AI along with other latest features that iPadOS 27 has to offer. This water-resistant design is only made possible with the improvements Apple made to the speakers, and Apple has come up with an innovative solution called the “Acoustic Display”, which translates to two front-facing speakers that allow for an even more immersive audio experience for entertainment, gaming, and editing purposes. The 12MP Center Stage camera now moves to the landscape edge, which is now ideal for video calls, and the iPad mini continues to feature the 12MP Wide back camera with Smart HDR 4 and Adaptive True Tone flash for convenient scanning. Following suit with other recent Apple products, the new iPad mini features the N1 wireless networking chip that consolidates Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread for the most up-to-date wireless connectivity. The N1 also performs more optimally when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the reliability of peer-to-peer features like AirPlay and AirDrop. The C2 cellular modem, which made its debut on the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo, also made its way to the cellular models of the new iPad mini, bringing up to 50% faster cellular data speeds over the previous generation. The new Smart Folio for this iPad mini is now redesigned with a two-panel architecture, and it’s crafted with a TechWoven fabric. Offered in both navy blue and taupe, this Smart Folio continues to bring great protection to the iPad mini while featuring a lightweight design that props up your iPad mini at different angles, perfect for watching your favorite content. The new iPad mini continues to support both the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro as well. The new iPad mini starts at $699, which is a $100 price increase over the previous generation, but considering all the improvements, especially that OLED display, it could’ve been more expensive as previously predicted. The new iPad mini is offered in these storage configurations (prices shown for the Wi-Fi model): The nano-texture option (for the 256GB and 512GB storage tiers) is available as a $100 upgrade, and cellular connectivity is available as a $150 upgrade. Pre-orders start this Wednesday (October 28) at 10:10 a.m. PT, and they’ll arrive in stores and to customers starting November 6.
