extraction.body: In October, Social Security recipients will learn what their cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, will be for 2027. The Social Security Administration announced its projected annual cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 Wednesday, with some recipients complaining the increase is not enough to offset soaring prices. So how much is it and what will it mean for checks? Benefits for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% in 2027. The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026. "The purpose of the COLA is to ensure that the purchasing power of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits is not eroded by inflation," the administration's website states. The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away. The agency's commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.” Still, the increase comes as the Bureau of Labor Statistics' released inflation data for September 2026, which showed the consumer price index rose 3.7% last month. The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income. To check your individual amount, notices will appear in Social Security accounts starting in late November and paper notices will go out about three weeks later. "Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center," the administration's website states. "Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online." The adjusted payments will not begin until January 2027. According to the agency, the cost-of-living adjustment "is based on the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) from the third quarter of the last year a COLA was determined to the third quarter of the current year." In other words, the COLA is automatically applied to benefits to help keep up with inflation. Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran. Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year's end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people. The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press. She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans' healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.” Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people. “There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan. Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town. Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance," given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country. “We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is," he said. Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices. The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress. The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits. While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same "would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times. The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy. Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program. The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill , gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren't able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold. Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

extraction.body: Mllions of Americans are set to receive their next Social Security payments in July, with the first round of checks scheduled to go out on July 2. The date matters because July 3, the usual payment day for some older beneficiaries, falls just before the Independence Day holiday weekend, meaning payments are being moved earlier. As per reporting by the New York Post, people who started receiving Social Security before May 1997 are due to be paid on Thursday, July 2. That same date also applies to many recipients who receive both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income. The rest of the July schedule depends on a beneficiary’s date of birth, with payments spread across three Wednesdays later in the month. The July 2 payment is for those who’ve been receiving Social Security benefits since before May 1997. SSI recipients are generally paid on the first day of the month, so those payments are expected on Wednesday, July 1, unless a recipient also falls into another payment category. After that, the Social Security Administration will follow its standard birthday-based schedule for retirement, disability, and survivor benefits. Those born between the 1st and 10th of any month should receive their July payment on Wednesday, July 8. Beneficiaries with birthdays between the 11th and 20th are scheduled to be paid on Wednesday, July 15, while those born between the 21st and 31st should receive checks on Wednesday, July 22. Some beneficiaries could receive payments of up to $5,181, as per reporting by Newsweek, although that maximum amount applies only to people who qualify based on work history, earnings, and when they chose to claim benefits. Most retirees receive less than the maximum monthly benefit, with individual payments varying depending on lifetime earnings and claiming age. Recipients who don’t receive their payment on the expected date are usually advised to check with their bank first, as processing times can vary. If the payment still hasn’t arrived after a short delay, beneficiaries can then contact the Social Security Administration for help. The July schedule also comes as more Americans rely on electronic payments, with direct deposit and government issued debit cards now central to how benefits are delivered.

extraction.body: Social Security payments in October have begun disbursing, and certain recipients will receive double payments this month. However, it’s not an extra payment. Here’s what’s going on with the calendar: The Supplemental Security Income program provides monthly income to eligible older adults who have little or no income, as well as to disabled individuals, which is different from Social Security's standard retirement benefits.SSI payments are ordinarily disbursed on the first of the month. But when the first of the month falls on a weekend or a federal holiday, SSI payments for that month are made on the last business day of the preceding month to ensure that beneficiaries have received their funds before the new month begins, and they face potential expenses.Due to the way the 2025 calendar falls, two SSI payments will go out in the month of October – one payment went out on Oct. 1 for October's benefits, while the second payment will go out on Friday, Oct. 31 for the month of November's benefits.RELATED: Social Security October payment schedule: Here’s when recipients get their checksThe government shutdown will not affect Social Security payments. RELATED: Does Social Security stop in government shutdown? extraction.body: Social Security recipients will see an “extra” payment this month — kind of. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is a program within Social Security , providing monthly checks to those with disabilities as well as older adults and disabled children. Millions of benefits are issued every month and are based on age or medical condition, limited income and few financial resources that factor into each check. And this month, checks will look a bit different. Recipients in October will see two payments thanks to a calendar quirk. The additional payment is for next month’s check, as Nov. 1 falls on a Sunday. This means SSI beneficiaries should expect to see their November green on Friday, Oct. 30. The early payment is not extra cash — and it’s quite typical. The SSA does not send payments on a weekend and SSI checks are always doled out on the first of every month. Since Nov. 1 is on a Sunday, this means checks will go out early — on Friday. Recipients will see an early check one more time this year in December. Since Jan. 1 is a holiday, folks will see two checks in December. The maximum monthly SSI payment for 2026 is $994 for an individual and $1,491 for a couple. To qualify for SSI, you must meet a few factors, according to the SSA . You must be a US citizen or national or a “noncitizen in one of certain alien classifications,” the SSA said. In addition, you must be at least 65, blind or disabled, have limited income and have limited resources. For more information on income levels and eligibility, head to the Social Security website . For those receiving Social Security , a program providing financial benefits to eligible workers after they reach retirement age, payments are staggered throughout the month and issued on Wednesdays, rolling out three times a month based on your birthday. For example, birthdays from the 1st-10th will get checks on the second Wednesday of each month. Birthdays 11th–20th will receive theirs on the third Wednesday of each month, while birthdays 21st–31st can expect theirs on the fourth Wednesday of each month. coreStoryFacts.text: In October, Social Security recipients will learn what their cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, will be for 2027.

"Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center," the administration's website states.
That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
To check your individual amount, notices will appear in Social Security accounts starting in late November and paper notices will go out about three weeks later.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September.
That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable.
Treating all income the same "would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes.
He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Benefits for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% in 2027.
The adjusted payments will not begin until January 2027.
As per reporting by the New York Post, people who started receiving Social Security before May 1997 are due to be paid on Thursday, July 2.
That same date also applies to many recipients who receive both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income.
SSI recipients are generally paid on the first day of the month, so those payments are expected on Wednesday, July 1, unless a recipient also falls into another payment category.
After that, the Social Security Administration will follow its standard birthday-based schedule for retirement, disability, and survivor benefits.
The date matters because July 3, the usual payment day for some older beneficiaries, falls just before the Independence Day holiday weekend, meaning payments are being moved earlier.
Recipients who don’t receive their payment on the expected date are usually advised to check with their bank first, as processing times can vary.

extraction.body: In October, Social Security recipients will learn what their cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, will be for 2027. The Social Security Administration announced its projected annual cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 Wednesday, with some recipients complaining the increase is not enough to offset soaring prices. So how much is it and what will it mean for checks? Benefits for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% in 2027. The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026. "The purpose of the COLA is to ensure that the purchasing power of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits is not eroded by inflation," the administration's website states. The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away. The agency's commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.” Still, the increase comes as the Bureau of Labor Statistics' released inflation data for September 2026, which showed the consumer price index rose 3.7% last month. The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income. To check your individual amount, notices will appear in Social Security accounts starting in late November and paper notices will go out about three weeks later. "Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center," the administration's website states. "Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online." The adjusted payments will not begin until January 2027. According to the agency, the cost-of-living adjustment "is based on the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) from the third quarter of the last year a COLA was determined to the third quarter of the current year." In other words, the COLA is automatically applied to benefits to help keep up with inflation. Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran. Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year's end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people. The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press. She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans' healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.” Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people. “There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan. Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town. Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance," given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country. “We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is," he said. Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices. The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress. The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits. While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same "would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times. The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy. Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program. The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill , gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren't able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold. Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

The date matters because July 3, the usual payment day for some older beneficiaries, falls just before the Independence Day holiday weekend, meaning payments are being moved earlier. As per reporting by the New York Post, people who started receiving Social Security before May 1997 are due to be paid on Thursday, July 2. The rest of the July schedule depends on a beneficiary’s date of birth, with payments spread across three Wednesdays later in the month. The July 2 payment is for those who’ve been receiving Social Security benefits since before May 1997. SSI recipients are generally paid on the first day of the month, so those payments are expected on Wednesday, July 1, unless a recipient also falls into another payment category. After that, the Social Security Administration will follow its standard birthday-based schedule for retirement, disability, and survivor benefits. Those born between the 1st and 10th of any month should receive their July payment on Wednesday, July 8. Beneficiaries with birthdays between the 11th and 20th are scheduled to be paid on Wednesday, July 15, while those born between the 21st and 31st should receive checks on Wednesday, July 22. Some beneficiaries could receive payments of up to $5,181, as per reporting by Newsweek, although that maximum amount applies only to people who qualify based on work history, earnings, and when they chose to claim benefits. Most retirees receive less than the maximum monthly benefit, with individual payments varying depending on lifetime earnings and claiming age. Recipients who don’t receive their payment on the expected date are usually advised to check with their bank first, as processing times can vary. If the payment still hasn’t arrived after a short delay, beneficiaries can then contact the Social Security Administration for help. The July schedule also comes as more Americans rely on electronic payments, with direct deposit and government issued debit cards now central to how benefits are delivered.

sources.title: Mars colony and Grok warnings: five strange details in SpaceX’s pitch to investors - The Guardian
passages: The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes.
Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”.
The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors.
Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises.

Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe.
Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February.
SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company.
It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services.
As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.
The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”.
Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material.
Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks.

The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options.
While outlining risk factors, SpaceX includes several large caveats surrounding its products and plans.
Such disclosures accounting for potential future risks and the uncertainty of guaranteed revenue are standard in IPO filings.
At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars .
The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels.
Elsewhere in the filing, SpaceX disclaims that, in order to make its vision successful, it will have to continue to pour more money into experimental and unproven technologies.

These big swings, core to its business, may simply not work out: “Many of the innovative products and services described elsewhere in this prospectus may ultimately be unsuccessful and may require great expense.”

passages: IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks
IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks

SpaceX publicly released an investor prospectus on Wednesday as part of its plan for a $1.75tn debut on the US stock market next month, revealing unseen details about the finances and future plans of Elon Musk ’s flagship company. In addition to new information on operating costs and revenue, the filing also included trademark Muskian sweeping proclamations about the universe and insights into some of the quirks of his tech empire.

Scattered throughout the 300-plus-page prospectus are several disclosures and risk warnings that show the eccentricities of Musk’s company and its cosmic ambitions. Other financial details in the document highlight how interdependent Musk’s various businesses have become and the risks that they carry.
As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.

SpaceX appears to have done extensive business with Tesla , spending hundreds of millions of dollars with Musk’s electric car company in recent years. Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks.

The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options. At that price, SpaceX would have acquired at least 1,300 vehicles.
Tesla only sold a total of 20,237 Cybertrucks last year, according to auto industry sales reports , meaning that SpaceX’s purchases made up a significant portion of its overall sales.

Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe.

“By moving beyond the only home we have ever known, we ensure species-level redundancy and that the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe,” the prospectus says. “We do not want humans to have the same fate as dinosaurs.”

At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars . The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels.

The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes. Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”.

The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors. Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises.

“We face a number of challenges relating to our business and growth strategy and, ultimately, the achievement of our mission to make life multiplanetary, understand the true nature of the universe, and extend the light of consciousness to the stars,” the prospectus reads.

The section of SpaceX’s filing that outlines risks to investors contains an array of legal and regulatory issues that reference various investigations, lawsuits and scandals involving Musk. Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February.

One passage in the prospectus discloses that xAI’s Grok chatbot, especially its “spicy” and “unhinged” modes, present a heightened risk of creating numerous harms including “the generation of potentially explicit content and misinformation or deceptive outputs, potential nonconsensual or exploitative imagery, intellectual property infringement, or content that could be viewed as exploitative, harmful, harassing, abusive, or discriminatory”.

The prospectus also states that the company is the subject of numerous domestic and international law enforcement investigations and inquiries related to allegations of Grok creating nonconsensual images.

Grok generated more than 3m sexualized images in the span of just 11 days earlier this year before the company increased some restrictions on its output, according to an estimate from the Center for Countering Digital Hate. The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”. Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material.

Musk has long expressed public concern about his personal safety and threats to his security. Through his private foundation and one of his top lieutenants, Musk has registered security companies in both California and Texas to provide him protection.

SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company. It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services.

Musk has repeatedly claimed that he frequently faces death threats and risks to his safety, especially during the period when he became the face of his “department of government efficiency” effort to gut federal agencies and humanitarian aid.

While outlining risk factors, SpaceX includes several large caveats surrounding its products and plans. The company disclosed that its massive amounts of spending have resulted in huge losses, including $4.9bn in 2025 and $4.3bn in the first quarter of this year alone. Such disclosures accounting for potential future risks and the uncertainty of guaranteed revenue are standard in IPO filings.
“We have a history of net losses and may not achieve profitability in the future,” the prospectus states.

Elsewhere in the filing, SpaceX disclaims that, in order to make its vision successful, it will have to continue to pour more money into experimental and unproven technologies. These big swings, core to its business, may simply not work out: “Many of the innovative products and services described elsewhere in this prospectus may ultimately be unsuccessful and may require great expense.”

extraction.body: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.
The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.
Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong.

For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges.
There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company.
It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering.

The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029.
Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.
Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.
It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation.
But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public.
Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters.
Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.
Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.

extraction.body: IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks SpaceX publicly released an investor prospectus on Wednesday as part of its plan for a $1.75tn debut on the US stock market next month, revealing unseen details about the finances and future plans of Elon Musk ’s flagship company. In addition to new information on operating costs and revenue, the filing also included trademark Muskian sweeping proclamations about the universe and insights into some of the quirks of his tech empire. Scattered throughout the 300-plus-page prospectus are several disclosures and risk warnings that show the eccentricities of Musk’s company and its cosmic ambitions. Other financial details in the document highlight how interdependent Musk’s various businesses have become and the risks that they carry. As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing. SpaceX appears to have done extensive business with Tesla , spending hundreds of millions of dollars with Musk’s electric car company in recent years. Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks. The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options. At that price, SpaceX would have acquired at least 1,300 vehicles. Tesla only sold a total of 20,237 Cybertrucks last year, according to auto industry sales reports , meaning that SpaceX’s purchases made up a significant portion of its overall sales. Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe. “By moving beyond the only home we have ever known, we ensure species-level redundancy and that the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe,” the prospectus says. “We do not want humans to have the same fate as dinosaurs.” At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars . The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels. The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes. Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”. The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors. Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises. “We face a number of challenges relating to our business and growth strategy and, ultimately, the achievement of our mission to make life multiplanetary, understand the true nature of the universe, and extend the light of consciousness to the stars,” the prospectus reads. The section of SpaceX’s filing that outlines risks to investors contains an array of legal and regulatory issues that reference various investigations, lawsuits and scandals involving Musk. Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February. One passage in the prospectus discloses that xAI’s Grok chatbot, especially its “spicy” and “unhinged” modes, present a heightened risk of creating numerous harms including “the generation of potentially explicit content and misinformation or deceptive outputs, potential nonconsensual or exploitative imagery, intellectual property infringement, or content that could be viewed as exploitative, harmful, harassing, abusive, or discriminatory”. passages: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.
Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela.

Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing.
It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation.
Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges.
Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.
Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.
It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering.

extraction.body: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

extraction.body: I’m reporting from the keynote speech by Philip W. Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, at Macworld Expo in San Francisco. We’ll keep updating this post for the duration of the speech, with the latest news at the top. Time stamps are New York time. 1:37 p.m.: More background: EMI had been the only one of the four major labels to offer DRM-free songs through iTunes Plus. The other three held out, demanding the right to set a range of prices for songs. They also wanted to spur the growth of Amazon’s MP3 store as a competitor to iTunes. But now Apple has given in on variable pricing, and is fully joining the DRM-free movement. 1:33 p.m.: Tony Bennett and his band emerge on a sliding stage. That’s a wrap folks. We’ll have more coverage of the implications of Apple’s move to variable pricing and DRM-free tracks later today. 1:32 p.m.: Starting today, iPhone owners can download songs over Wi-Fi and 3G networks. So you no longer need to connect your iPhone to a computer or be on a Wi-Fi network to buy songs. ( UPDATE: Fixed this paragraph to reflect the fact that song downloads over Wi-Fi were already available.) 1:29 p.m.: Mr. Schiller notes that iTunes Plus has been a way for Apple to offer music that is free of digital rights management software, which restricts copying. Those songs can be transferred to as many computers and devices as users choose. Apple will now offer 8 million songs in iTunes Plus and add 2 million more by the end of the quarter. So all 10 million songs will be DRM-free by the spring. It appears Apple will charge people to remove the DRM from their existing library. We are going to need more details on this later — Mr. Schiller went through that very fast. 1:27 p.m.: Apple is moving to variable pricing, Mr. Schiller reports. Instead of 99 cents for all songs, there will be two new pricing tiers: 69 cents and $1.29, for older and more popular tracks respectively. Music labels get to choose their tier. That begins in April. 1:26 p.m.: The iTunes store has sold 6 billion songs since 2003, Mr. Schiller reports. There are 10 million songs available on iTunes, and 75 million people have registered with their credit cards there. ITunes of course is the No. 1 channel for music, ahead of Wal-Mart and Amazon.com. 1:25 p.m.: The new 17-inch MacBook Pro costs $2,799. Not a very economical choice for these frugal times. And finally, One Last Thing, concerning iTunes. 1:21 p.m.: The new battery cannot be removed or swapped out and saves some space as a result. More space equals more energy storage capacity. The bottom line: Apple is promising 60 percent more battery life than comparable MacBooks, and a highly recyclable machine overall. At this point in the presentation, everyone here must be thinking the same thing: Um, is that it? Let’s see if it is… 1:05 p.m.: And that completes iWork ’09. It’s $79, or $99 for a family pack. If you purchase it with a new Mac it’s $49. It starts shipping today. Mr. Schiller said Apple is also bringing iWork into the cloud, with a new service called iWork.com that allows people to share documents with others online. We’re getting a demo of iWork.com now. 1:00 p.m.: After a demo of Pages ’09, the word processor, we’re on to Numbers ’09, Apple’s spreadsheet program. Mr. Schiller said the company was adding new advanced features, like more flexible tables and new chart options, to bring the program up to par with some of the more established alternatives. 12:57 p.m.: Mr. Schiller is talking about the new transitions and animations in Keynote ’09, Apple’s version of PowerPoint. Suddenly I am thinking wistfully about that novel I never finished in college. 12:03 p.m.: At the Moscone Center, waiting for the PhilNote ! 9:30 a.m.: In today’s performance, the part normally played by Steven P. Jobs, Apple’s co-founder and chief executive, will be played by Philip W. Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide product marketing. Greetings, and welcome to Apple’s keynote presentation at the Macworld 2009 conference in San Francisco. As you no doubt read already in the program, there has been a change in the cast. Steve Jobs will not be delivering today’s speech, and after this year, Apple will not be taking part in this overhyped annual conference at all anymore. You can blame the company’s diminishing tolerance for a grueling post-holiday January ritual, or Mr. Jobs’s health , but the fact remains that at noon Eastern time, Apple’s marketing guru, Phil Schiller, will take the stage. Try not to look disappointed. There may be a few surprises in store yet. The Apple watchers think they already know the script to this show. They expect a refreshed line of iMacs, with Nvidia chips for sharper graphics and video, and perhaps a lower price to make Apple’s line of desktop computers more appealing to the frugal masses in a deep recession year. We will no doubt hear about upgrades to Apple’s Mac OS X operating system, and perhaps to its somewhat overlooked television set-top box, AppleTV. Could we see new deals with the major music labels to put unprotected music files on iTunes and allow direct, over-the-air downloads to the iPhone? Some think so . And how about that elusive Macintosh laptop with no keyboard ? In short, expectations are set fairly low today. 1:29 p.m.: Mr. Schiller notes that iTunes Plus has been a way for Apple to offer music that is free of digital rights management software, which restricts copying. Those songs can be transferred to as many computers and devices as users choose. Apple will now offer 8 million songs in iTunes Plus and add 2 million more by the end of the quarter. passages: Apple Event 2026 is set to take place on September 9, with the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and Apple’s first foldable iPhone expected to headline the company’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ showcase.
The event begins at 10:00 am PT, or 10:30 pm IST, and viewers can watch it through Apple’s official YouTube livestream or Apple TV.
This live story will track the latest Apple event updates, expected launches and confirmed announcements as they happen.
The foldable iPhone is expected, but its final name is unclear.
The Apple Watch Series 12, Watch Ultra 4 and AirPods 5 are also potential launches rather than confirmed products at this stage.
A camera feature would appear more likely for a future AirPods Pro model, though Apple could still have surprises in store under John Ternus’ first major product event as CEO.
The biggest expectation is Apple’s entry into foldable smartphones.
Following the pandemic in 2020, the company largely shifted its product introductions to pre-recorded video presentations.
The report adds two important details to the pre-launch picture: a possible iPhone Duo branding and a $2,000 price point for Apple’s foldable device.
Until now, the handset had appeared under multiple possible names in pre-event reports, including iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra and iPhone Duo.
It is also expected to be the first major launch event of a new leadership era at Apple.
Apple is unlikely to introduce camera-equipped AirPods at today’s event, with current rumours pointing to a relatively modest AirPods 5 update instead.

Reports cited ahead of the event also suggest that the foldable could use Samsung display technology designed to minimise the visible crease on the inner folding screen.
Executives have appeared around those presentations in subsequent years, but this event is expected to mark a return to the more traditional stage-led launch format.
Apple has not confirmed the reason for the store outage, so for now it should be treated as a pre-event observation rather than an official announcement.

passages: Apple has had a busy fall, with the launch of the iPhone Duo, HomeView smart hub, and the M5 Ultra Mac Studio.
But there’s one more event this week, and it might be the biggest of all.
And you can follow every rumor and announcement with us right here.
That probably means we’re getting the M6 iMac and M6 MacBook Pro tomorrow and the touchscreen MacBook Pro on Wednesday.

While the iPad mini has all the makings of a pro device, with an OLED display, A20 Pro processor, and refined color palette, but it’s still missing one major feature of Apple’s other Pro devices: 120Hz ProMotion.
There were scattered reports that Apple would be bringing the high-end screen tech to the mini along with its OLED upgrade, but alas, it didn’t make the cut.
Looks like we’ll have to wait another 2-3 years.
That’s a bunch of firsts for a non-Pro iPad and a massive upgrade.
The screen is now 8.5 inches (up from 8.3 inches) and the camera is now on the landscape edge.
It also got a price hike, but not as bad as feared: $699.
Apple has hidden a pretty nice upgrade in the tech specs.
But if you opt for the 512GB model you get the full version of the chip, with a 6-core CPU and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.
iPad owners (with the exception of iPad Pro owners, who are a whole different breed) tend not to worry too much about tech specs.
But I would argue that cutting-edge AI performance is a pretty low priority for most of the mini’s prospective customers.
Since Apple has only announced one day of announcements, one of three things could happen today: An iPad mini announcement at 9 am ET, 1 pm ET, or nothing at all.

coreStoryFacts.text: Schiller notes that iTunes Plus has been a way for Apple to offer music that is free of digital rights management software, which restricts copying.
Those songs can be transferred to as many computers and devices as users choose.
Apple will now offer 8 million songs in iTunes Plus and add 2 million more by the end of the quarter.
I’m reporting from the keynote speech by Philip W.
Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, at Macworld Expo in San Francisco.
We’ll keep updating this post for the duration of the speech, with the latest news at the top.
1:27 p.m.: Apple is moving to variable pricing, Mr.
Instead of 99 cents for all songs, there will be two new pricing tiers: 69 cents and $1.29, for older and more popular tracks respectively.
Could we see new deals with the major music labels to put unprotected music files on iTunes and allow direct, over-the-air downloads to the iPhone?
1:21 p.m.: The new battery cannot be removed or swapped out and saves some space as a result.
More space equals more energy storage capacity.
The bottom line: Apple is promising 60 percent more battery life than comparable MacBooks, and a highly recyclable machine overall.
The other three held out, demanding the right to set a range of prices for songs.
They also wanted to spur the growth of Amazon’s MP3 store as a competitor to iTunes.
But now Apple has given in on variable pricing, and is fully joining the DRM-free movement.
Suddenly I am thinking wistfully about that novel I never finished in college.
Steve Jobs will not be delivering today’s speech, and after this year, Apple will not be taking part in this overhyped annual conference at all anymore.
You can blame the company’s diminishing tolerance for a grueling post-holiday January ritual, or Mr.
Schiller said the company was adding new advanced features, like more flexible tables and new chart options, to bring the program up to par with some of the more established alternatives.
1:33 p.m.: Tony Bennett and his band emerge on a sliding stage.
Schiller said Apple is also bringing iWork into the cloud, with a new service called iWork.com that allows people to share documents with others online.
We’re getting a demo of iWork.com now.
The Apple watchers think they already know the script to this show.
One way Apple could surprise everyone and reap a torrent of fawning news coverage is through an appearance by Mr.

extraction.body: I’m reporting from the keynote speech by Philip W. Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, at Macworld Expo in San Francisco. We’ll keep updating this post for the duration of the speech, with the latest news at the top. Time stamps are New York time. 1:37 p.m.: More background: EMI had been the only one of the four major labels to offer DRM-free songs through iTunes Plus. The other three held out, demanding the right to set a range of prices for songs. They also wanted to spur the growth of Amazon’s MP3 store as a competitor to iTunes. But now Apple has given in on variable pricing, and is fully joining the DRM-free movement. 1:33 p.m.: Tony Bennett and his band emerge on a sliding stage. That’s a wrap folks. We’ll have more coverage of the implications of Apple’s move to variable pricing and DRM-free tracks later today. 1:32 p.m.: Starting today, iPhone owners can download songs over Wi-Fi and 3G networks. So you no longer need to connect your iPhone to a computer or be on a Wi-Fi network to buy songs. ( UPDATE: Fixed this paragraph to reflect the fact that song downloads over Wi-Fi were already available.) 1:29 p.m.: Mr. Schiller notes that iTunes Plus has been a way for Apple to offer music that is free of digital rights management software, which restricts copying. Those songs can be transferred to as many computers and devices as users choose. Apple will now offer 8 million songs in iTunes Plus and add 2 million more by the end of the quarter. So all 10 million songs will be DRM-free by the spring. It appears Apple will charge people to remove the DRM from their existing library. We are going to need more details on this later — Mr. Schiller went through that very fast. 1:27 p.m.: Apple is moving to variable pricing, Mr. Schiller reports. Instead of 99 cents for all songs, there will be two new pricing tiers: 69 cents and $1.29, for older and more popular tracks respectively. Music labels get to choose their tier. That begins in April. 1:26 p.m.: The iTunes store has sold 6 billion songs since 2003, Mr. Schiller reports. There are 10 million songs available on iTunes, and 75 million people have registered with their credit cards there. ITunes of course is the No. 1 channel for music, ahead of Wal-Mart and Amazon.com. 1:25 p.m.: The new 17-inch MacBook Pro costs $2,799. Not a very economical choice for these frugal times. And finally, One Last Thing, concerning iTunes. 1:21 p.m.: The new battery cannot be removed or swapped out and saves some space as a result. More space equals more energy storage capacity. The bottom line: Apple is promising 60 percent more battery life than comparable MacBooks, and a highly recyclable machine overall. At this point in the presentation, everyone here must be thinking the same thing: Um, is that it? Let’s see if it is… 1:05 p.m.: And that completes iWork ’09. It’s $79, or $99 for a family pack. If you purchase it with a new Mac it’s $49. It starts shipping today. Mr. Schiller said Apple is also bringing iWork into the cloud, with a new service called iWork.com that allows people to share documents with others online. We’re getting a demo of iWork.com now. 1:00 p.m.: After a demo of Pages ’09, the word processor, we’re on to Numbers ’09, Apple’s spreadsheet program. Mr. Schiller said the company was adding new advanced features, like more flexible tables and new chart options, to bring the program up to par with some of the more established alternatives. 12:57 p.m.: Mr. Schiller is talking about the new transitions and animations in Keynote ’09, Apple’s version of PowerPoint. Suddenly I am thinking wistfully about that novel I never finished in college. 12:03 p.m.: At the Moscone Center, waiting for the PhilNote ! 9:30 a.m.: In today’s performance, the part normally played by Steven P. Jobs, Apple’s co-founder and chief executive, will be played by Philip W. Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide product marketing. Greetings, and welcome to Apple’s keynote presentation at the Macworld 2009 conference in San Francisco. As you no doubt read already in the program, there has been a change in the cast. Steve Jobs will not be delivering today’s speech, and after this year, Apple will not be taking part in this overhyped annual conference at all anymore. You can blame the company’s diminishing tolerance for a grueling post-holiday January ritual, or Mr. Jobs’s health , but the fact remains that at noon Eastern time, Apple’s marketing guru, Phil Schiller, will take the stage. Try not to look disappointed. There may be a few surprises in store yet. The Apple watchers think they already know the script to this show. They expect a refreshed line of iMacs, with Nvidia chips for sharper graphics and video, and perhaps a lower price to make Apple’s line of desktop computers more appealing to the frugal masses in a deep recession year. We will no doubt hear about upgrades to Apple’s Mac OS X operating system, and perhaps to its somewhat overlooked television set-top box, AppleTV. Could we see new deals with the major music labels to put unprotected music files on iTunes and allow direct, over-the-air downloads to the iPhone? Some think so . And how about that elusive Macintosh laptop with no keyboard ? In short, expectations are set fairly low today. One way Apple could surprise everyone and reap a torrent of fawning news coverage is through an appearance by Mr. Jobs himself. I think it could happen — Monday’s health news was interestingly timed, as if the company were trying to pre-empt any negative reactions to an appearance by Mr. Jobs at the conference. If I’m wrong on that, well, I won’t be alone. Incorrect speculation is normal before every Apple show. “We’re getting a demo of the upgraded iMovie. Folks, talk amongst yourselves…” Jeez, Brad Stone, if you’re bored by one of the unique Mac iLife apps, maybe there’s someone else there who’s interested in actual liveblogging? Where’s Pogue when you need him? I was hoping for a different perspective rather than no perspective… so it’s off to Macworld’s posts for me. I agree with #2. Next time, NYT, have someone who is actually interested in reporting on the updates do the liveblogging. I checked elsewhere for an account of the iMovie news, and I think I’ll just do the rest of my refreshes there. They just announced an iNtergalactic space decoder. Snappy, too. This has to be lamest Macworld ever. Nobody in the audience came to see an update to iLife, iWork and Macbook Pro. Maybe Steve does not trust Phil to launch a new product or a major upgrade. Tier pricing for iTunes Music. So dumb! But what else do you expect from the minds of record company execs. No iPhone nano… No 64GB iPod touch… No details on Snow Leopard… And, most significantly, no Steve Jobs presenting the keynote… This has got to be the absolute WORST MacWorld ever to have taken place. Doesn’t it make sense that more popular/higher demand songs should cost more than more obscure/lower demand songs? The blogger seems completely uninterested and I wouldn’t be surprised if they have never owned an apple product in their lifetime. Their snide remarks show that they have no previous knowledge of the products and how far the company has come, and what these improvements mean. I think folks are getting a bit too rabid in their complaints about this liveblog. Yes, folks like Engadget do a better job (teams taking screenshots, etc.), and I would have preferred fewer gratuitous shots (iPhoto makes his old iMac run slowly — sheesh, how well does Lightroom run on it?). What I expect from the NYT will hopefully come later today: a serious article putting these announcements in context. For example, how will Apple do in the Convergence space without a new Mini? Why no demo of Snow Leopard? How does iPhoto stack up against today’s newly-announced beta of Picasa3 for the Mac?

1:26 p.m.: The iTunes store has sold 6 billion songs since 2003, Mr. Schiller reports. There are 10 million songs available on iTunes, and 75 million people have registered with their credit cards there. ITunes of course is the No. 1 channel for music, ahead of Wal-Mart and Amazon.com.
1:25 p.m.: The new 17-inch MacBook Pro costs $2,799. Not a very economical choice for these frugal times.
And finally, One Last Thing, concerning iTunes.

1:21 p.m.: The new battery cannot be removed or swapped out and saves some space as a result. More space equals more energy storage capacity. The bottom line: Apple is promising 60 percent more battery life than comparable MacBooks, and a highly recyclable machine overall.
At this point in the presentation, everyone here must be thinking the same thing: Um, is that it? Let’s see if it is…
1:05 p.m.: And that completes iWork ’09. It’s $79, or $99 for a family pack. If you purchase it with a new Mac it’s $49. It starts shipping today.
Mr. Schiller said Apple is also bringing iWork into the cloud, with a new service called iWork.com that allows people to share documents with others online. We’re getting a demo of iWork.com now.

1:00 p.m.: After a demo of Pages ’09, the word processor, we’re on to Numbers ’09, Apple’s spreadsheet program. Mr. Schiller said the company was adding new advanced features, like more flexible tables and new chart options, to bring the program up to par with some of the more established alternatives.

12:57 p.m.: Mr. Schiller is talking about the new transitions and animations in Keynote ’09, Apple’s version of PowerPoint. Suddenly I am thinking wistfully about that novel I never finished in college.
12:03 p.m.: At the Moscone Center, waiting for the PhilNote !

9:30 a.m.: In today’s performance, the part normally played by Steven P. Jobs, Apple’s co-founder and chief executive, will be played by Philip W. Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide product marketing.

Greetings, and welcome to Apple’s keynote presentation at the Macworld 2009 conference in San Francisco. As you no doubt read already in the program, there has been a change in the cast. Steve Jobs will not be delivering today’s speech, and after this year, Apple will not be taking part in this overhyped annual conference at all anymore. You can blame the company’s diminishing tolerance for a grueling post-holiday January ritual, or Mr. Jobs’s health , but the fact remains that at noon Eastern time, Apple’s marketing guru, Phil Schiller, will take the stage. Try not to look disappointed. There may be a few surprises in store yet.

The Apple watchers think they already know the script to this show. They expect a refreshed line of iMacs, with Nvidia chips for sharper graphics and video, and perhaps a lower price to make Apple’s line of desktop computers more appealing to the frugal masses in a deep recession year.

We will no doubt hear about upgrades to Apple’s Mac OS X operating system, and perhaps to its somewhat overlooked television set-top box, AppleTV. Could we see new deals with the major music labels to put unprotected music files on iTunes and allow direct, over-the-air downloads to the iPhone? Some think so .
And how about that elusive Macintosh laptop with no keyboard ?
In short, expectations are set fairly low today.

One way Apple could surprise everyone and reap a torrent of fawning news coverage is through an appearance by Mr. Jobs himself. I think it could happen — Monday’s health news was interestingly timed, as if the company were trying to pre-empt any negative reactions to an appearance by Mr. Jobs at the conference.
If I’m wrong on that, well, I won’t be alone. Incorrect speculation is normal before every Apple show.
“We’re getting a demo of the upgraded iMovie. Folks, talk amongst yourselves…”

Jeez, Brad Stone, if you’re bored by one of the unique Mac iLife apps, maybe there’s someone else there who’s interested in actual liveblogging? Where’s Pogue when you need him? I was hoping for a different perspective rather than no perspective… so it’s off to Macworld’s posts for me.

I agree with #2. Next time, NYT, have someone who is actually interested in reporting on the updates do the liveblogging. I checked elsewhere for an account of the iMovie news, and I think I’ll just do the rest of my refreshes there.
They just announced an iNtergalactic space decoder. Snappy, too.
This has to be lamest Macworld ever. Nobody in the audience came to see an update to iLife, iWork and Macbook Pro. Maybe Steve does not trust Phil to launch a new product or a major upgrade.
Tier pricing for iTunes Music. So dumb! But what else do you expect from the minds of record company execs.
No iPhone nano… No 64GB iPod touch… No details on Snow Leopard… And, most significantly, no Steve Jobs presenting the keynote… This has got to be the absolute WORST MacWorld ever to have taken place.
Doesn’t it make sense that more popular/higher demand songs should cost more than more obscure/lower demand songs?

The blogger seems completely uninterested and I wouldn’t be surprised if they have never owned an apple product in their lifetime. Their snide remarks show that they have no previous knowledge of the products and how far the company has come, and what these improvements mean.

I think folks are getting a bit too rabid in their complaints about this liveblog. Yes, folks like Engadget do a better job (teams taking screenshots, etc.), and I would have preferred fewer gratuitous shots (iPhoto makes his old iMac run slowly — sheesh, how well does Lightroom run on it?).

What I expect from the NYT will hopefully come later today: a serious article putting these announcements in context. For example, how will Apple do in the Convergence space without a new Mini? Why no demo of Snow Leopard? How does iPhoto stack up against today’s newly-announced beta of Picasa3 for the Mac?

passages: Apple has had a busy fall, with the launch of the iPhone Duo, HomeView smart hub, and the M5 Ultra Mac Studio.
But there’s one more event this week, and it might be the biggest of all.
And you can follow every rumor and announcement with us right here.
That probably means we’re getting the M6 iMac and M6 MacBook Pro tomorrow and the touchscreen MacBook Pro on Wednesday.

While the iPad mini has all the makings of a pro device, with an OLED display, A20 Pro processor, and refined color palette, but it’s still missing one major feature of Apple’s other Pro devices: 120Hz ProMotion.
There were scattered reports that Apple would be bringing the high-end screen tech to the mini along with its OLED upgrade, but alas, it didn’t make the cut.
Looks like we’ll have to wait another 2-3 years.
That’s a bunch of firsts for a non-Pro iPad and a massive upgrade.
The screen is now 8.5 inches (up from 8.3 inches) and the camera is now on the landscape edge.
It also got a price hike, but not as bad as feared: $699.
Apple has hidden a pretty nice upgrade in the tech specs.
But if you opt for the 512GB model you get the full version of the chip, with a 6-core CPU and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.
iPad owners (with the exception of iPad Pro owners, who are a whole different breed) tend not to worry too much about tech specs.
But I would argue that cutting-edge AI performance is a pretty low priority for most of the mini’s prospective customers.
Since Apple has only announced one day of announcements, one of three things could happen today: An iPad mini announcement at 9 am ET, 1 pm ET, or nothing at all.
How will Apple sell its new touchscreen Mac to the public?
According to Mark Gurman , it will be billed as an “optional” feature rather than a primary one, not unlike the Touch Bar.
We know there won’t be a keynote, but we don’t know if Apple will spread out its launches throughout the week as it has done in the past.
So come back each day to check out what you missed!
Michael Simon has been covering Apple for more than 20 years.
He started covering rumors with Spymac when the iPod was the iWalk, and has owned nearly every iPhone Apple has ever made.
He lives in Connecticut with his wife, son, and far too many gadgets.
This week could see Apple add a third entry to that list.

But there’s one more event this week, and it might be the biggest of all. And you can follow every rumor and announcement with us right here. Apple kicked off its week of releases with the new iPad mini , which got a thinner design, new A20 Pro chip, and an OLED display. As you can guess by the thinly veiled pun, this week’s marquee announcement is a new MacBook Pro, but not just any MacBook Pro. Here’s what else we’re expecting to see: Touchscreen MacBook Pro: After years of denials, Apple appears to be on the verge of releasing its first-ever touchscreen MacBook . Rumors say it will have a new design with a lighter chassis, Dynamic Island, and an OLED display. And a very high price tag. M6 iMac: Apple announced the M6 chip in the Mac mini last month and now it’ll reportedly make its way into the iMac . There could be new colors too.
