extraction.body: "Good morning. Thank you to Colombia, and Security Council President Ambassador Leonor Zalabata, for convening this important debate. "Thank you also to the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, Vanessa Frazier, and to the civil society representative, for their briefings. "A school … a hospital ... a water point ... should never be a battlefield. And no child should have to wonder whether entering a classroom or health facility might cost her life. "Yet for millions of children living through conflict, that is precisely the reality they face every single day. "The Secretary-General's latest report on Children and Armed Conflict documents 38,558 verified grave violations against children in 2025. Behind that number are children killed and maimed … recruited and used by armed forces and armed groups … abducted … subjected to sexual violence … denied humanitarian assistance … and deprived of education, health, and protection. "These alarming figures tell only part of the story. "We must act with the urgency and consistency that this reality demands. "In my missions with UNICEF, I have met children who have fled their homes and communities because of conflict … children who witnessed the killing of family members, friends, and neighbors … and girls who were subjected to horrific sexual violence by armed actors. "Their experiences remind us that every verified violation in this report represents a child whose safety, dignity, and future have been profoundly affected. "In addition to causing harm, these weapons destroy schools, hospitals, water systems, power networks, and other civilian infrastructure essential for children's survival and recovery. They leave behind unexploded ordnance that can continue to kill and maim children years after hostilities have ended. "Parties to conflict must protect civilians … and must not use explosive weapons in populated areas. States must strengthen—not weaken—the international frameworks designed to protect civilians, including children. "A second alarming trend is the growing number of children subjected to multiple grave violations. In 2025, this number increased again, to more than 3,100 children. "This means that a child has had several terrible things happen to them. They are abducted or recruited, and in many cases, also subjected to rape or other forms of sexual violence. "Even amid these troubling trends, there are some reasons for hope. The Children and Armed Conflict agenda continues to demonstrate that progress is possible. "In 2025, more than 13,000 children left armed forces or armed groups. These children received reintegration and protection support from UNICEF and our partners. "Governments and non-State armed groups engaged with the United Nations … negotiated commitments … implemented preventive measures … and took steps to release children and prevent future violations. "In Colombia, for example, the Government has strengthened prevention measures against recruitment and use, sexual violence, and attacks affecting education. These efforts include the adoption of prevention strategies and guidelines for school risk management and education in emergencies. "In Haiti, authorities launched initiatives to prevent recruitment by armed groups, and to support the reintegration of affected children. "And in Syria, the Government has committed to preventing the recruitment and use of children … and is working with the United Nations on strengthening its protection commitments. "Important engagement has also continued in Mozambique, Libya, Somalia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Yemen, South Sudan, and Sudan. "Allow me to conclude with six recommendations. "First, Member States must use their influence to ensure that all parties to conflict adhere to their obligations to respect international humanitarian law and international human rights law. In light of the information contained in this report, no one can plead ignorance about the impact of war on children. "Political, military, financial, and other forms of support should be informed by robust assessments of the risks to children. Where risks are identified, support should be accompanied by concrete measures to prevent, mitigate, and address harm. "States should also avoid transferring weapons when there is a clear risk they could be used to commit or enable grave violations against children. "Second, all parties in conflict must take concrete steps to protect children. "This includes protecting schools, students, teachers, and education personnel … ending attacks on education … refraining from the military use of schools … issuing clear command orders to protect education … and ensuring accountability for violations. "They should be released promptly and transferred to civilian child protection actors for care, family reunification, and reintegration. "Fourth, the Security Council must continue to defend and strengthen the Children and Armed Conflict agenda. "This includes preserving the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism … ensuring that decisions remain evidence-based … maintaining a timely and fully functioning Working Group … and using all available tools to press parties to engage with the agenda and protect children. "The rise in attacks on humanitarian personnel and the increasing denial of humanitarian access is appalling and should prompt urgent action by this Council. "Finally, Member States should strengthen the legal and policy frameworks that protect children in armed conflict. "This requires continued commitment to treaties that have helped reduce civilian harm, including the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, and the Convention on Cluster Munitions. "At a time when children are facing unprecedented levels of harm in conflict, the Children and Armed Conflict agenda needs strong political and financial support. "Funding cuts are weakening child protection capacities precisely when needs are growing. They are reducing support for children affected by grave violations … including family tracing and reunification, mental health and psychosocial support, reintegration services, survivor-centred care, and safe access to education and healthcare. "Protecting children cannot be a peripheral concern of peace and security. UNICEF, the United Nations agency for children, works to protect the rights of every child, everywhere, especially the most disadvantaged children and in the toughest places to reach. Across more than 190 countries and territories, we do whatever it takes to help children survive, thrive, and fulfil their potential. Follow UNICEF on X , Facebook , Instagram and YouTube

extraction.body: "Good morning. Thank you to Colombia, and Security Council President Ambassador Leonor Zalabata, for convening this important debate. "Thank you also to the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, Vanessa Frazier, and to the civil society representative, for their briefings. "A school … a hospital ... a water point ... should never be a battlefield. And no child should have to wonder whether entering a classroom or health facility might cost her life. "Yet for millions of children living through conflict, that is precisely the reality they face every single day. "The Secretary-General's latest report on Children and Armed Conflict documents 38,558 verified grave violations against children in 2025. Behind that number are children killed and maimed … recruited and used by armed forces and armed groups … abducted … subjected to sexual violence … denied humanitarian assistance … and deprived of education, health, and protection. "These alarming figures tell only part of the story. "We must act with the urgency and consistency that this reality demands. "In my missions with UNICEF, I have met children who have fled their homes and communities because of conflict … children who witnessed the killing of family members, friends, and neighbors … and girls who were subjected to horrific sexual violence by armed actors. "Their experiences remind us that every verified violation in this report represents a child whose safety, dignity, and future have been profoundly affected. "In addition to causing harm, these weapons destroy schools, hospitals, water systems, power networks, and other civilian infrastructure essential for children's survival and recovery. They leave behind unexploded ordnance that can continue to kill and maim children years after hostilities have ended. "Parties to conflict must protect civilians … and must not use explosive weapons in populated areas. States must strengthen—not weaken—the international frameworks designed to protect civilians, including children. "A second alarming trend is the growing number of children subjected to multiple grave violations. In 2025, this number increased again, to more than 3,100 children. "This means that a child has had several terrible things happen to them. They are abducted or recruited, and in many cases, also subjected to rape or other forms of sexual violence. "Even amid these troubling trends, there are some reasons for hope. The Children and Armed Conflict agenda continues to demonstrate that progress is possible. "In 2025, more than 13,000 children left armed forces or armed groups. These children received reintegration and protection support from UNICEF and our partners. "Governments and non-State armed groups engaged with the United Nations … negotiated commitments … implemented preventive measures … and took steps to release children and prevent future violations. "In Colombia, for example, the Government has strengthened prevention measures against recruitment and use, sexual violence, and attacks affecting education. These efforts include the adoption of prevention strategies and guidelines for school risk management and education in emergencies. "In Haiti, authorities launched initiatives to prevent recruitment by armed groups, and to support the reintegration of affected children. "And in Syria, the Government has committed to preventing the recruitment and use of children … and is working with the United Nations on strengthening its protection commitments. "Important engagement has also continued in Mozambique, Libya, Somalia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Yemen, South Sudan, and Sudan. "Allow me to conclude with six recommendations. "First, Member States must use their influence to ensure that all parties to conflict adhere to their obligations to respect international humanitarian law and international human rights law. In light of the information contained in this report, no one can plead ignorance about the impact of war on children. "Political, military, financial, and other forms of support should be informed by robust assessments of the risks to children. Where risks are identified, support should be accompanied by concrete measures to prevent, mitigate, and address harm. "States should also avoid transferring weapons when there is a clear risk they could be used to commit or enable grave violations against children. "Second, all parties in conflict must take concrete steps to protect children. "This includes protecting schools, students, teachers, and education personnel … ending attacks on education … refraining from the military use of schools … issuing clear command orders to protect education … and ensuring accountability for violations. "They should be released promptly and transferred to civilian child protection actors for care, family reunification, and reintegration. "Fourth, the Security Council must continue to defend and strengthen the Children and Armed Conflict agenda. "This includes preserving the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism … ensuring that decisions remain evidence-based … maintaining a timely and fully functioning Working Group … and using all available tools to press parties to engage with the agenda and protect children. "The rise in attacks on humanitarian personnel and the increasing denial of humanitarian access is appalling and should prompt urgent action by this Council. "Finally, Member States should strengthen the legal and policy frameworks that protect children in armed conflict. "This requires continued commitment to treaties that have helped reduce civilian harm, including the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, and the Convention on Cluster Munitions. "At a time when children are facing unprecedented levels of harm in conflict, the Children and Armed Conflict agenda needs strong political and financial support. "Funding cuts are weakening child protection capacities precisely when needs are growing. They are reducing support for children affected by grave violations … including family tracing and reunification, mental health and psychosocial support, reintegration services, survivor-centred care, and safe access to education and healthcare. "Protecting children cannot be a peripheral concern of peace and security. UNICEF, the United Nations agency for children, works to protect the rights of every child, everywhere, especially the most disadvantaged children and in the toughest places to reach. Across more than 190 countries and territories, we do whatever it takes to help children survive, thrive, and fulfil their potential. Follow UNICEF on X , Facebook , Instagram and YouTube

sources.title: T-Mobile’s new plans include swappable subscription perks
passages: T-Mobile is launching new “T-Mix” plans that bundle wireless service with subscriptions to services like Netflix, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, device promotions, and more, as reported earlier by Fierce Network.
However, T-Mobile notes that how often you can change your perks depends on the benefit that you choose.
“Some benefits let you switch any time, others hold your Picks for a quarter or longer,” T-Mobile says, adding that some services will charge if you switch them outside the change window.

extraction.body: T-Mobile is launching new “T-Mix” plans that bundle wireless service with subscriptions to services like Netflix, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, device promotions, and more, as reported earlier by Fierce Network. The Standard plan starts at $55 / month (with autopay) for one line and one “Pick,” which you can change up to four times during the year without changing the cost of your plan. Meanwhile, the mid-tier More plan starts at $75 / month for one line, two Picks per line, and unlimited data. The Loaded plan also comes with the same up to 4K UHD video streaming benefit, as well as up to 250GB of high-speed hotspot data and up to 30GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico. The types of perks you can add vary depending on how many your plan supports: * One Pick: Apple TV, DashPass by DoorDash, Google AI Plus, Hulu with ads, Netflix Standard with ads, Pandora Plus, Paramount Plus Essential, SiriusXM All Access (app only), YouTube Premium Lite, 500 miles / month through Delta SkyMiles, T-Satellite * Two Picks: Apple Music Individual, Google AI Pro, Pandora Premium, Xbox Game Pass Premium, YouTube Premium * Three Picks: Netflix Standard, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate * Four Picks: ESPN Unlimited, Netflix Premium As noted by CNET, you can also trade your Picks for discounts on a new phone. T-Mobile says that you can change up your perks every 90 days, according to Fierce Network. However, T-Mobile notes that how often you can change your perks depends on the benefit that you choose. “Some benefits let you switch any time, others hold your Picks for a quarter or longer,” T-Mobile says, adding that some services will charge if you switch them outside the change window. T-Mobile also offers an annual selection period where you can reset all of your perks.

EE is launching the ultimate unlimited data plans on the best mobile network in the UK as rated by independent testing experts RootMetrics, for the sixth year running. Created for customers who want a completely unlimited experience, the new EE unlimited data plans come with no speed restrictions and are available today for 4G and 5G SIM-only and smartphone plan customers from EE shops, over the phone and on ee.co.uk.

Customers who want the ultimate smartphone experience on the UK’s first 5G network, can now take a 5G unlimited Smart Plan. As well as access to 5G, customers will never run out of great entertainment on the go, with the option to add an inclusive Amazon Prime Video subscription, HDR BT Sports App access and Roam Further Pass for the duration of their plan. This gives customers access to more than £25 worth of EE benefits each month, letting them watch movies, original TV shows and live sport on the go, all on EE’s award-winning network.

Customers with an unlimited 5G Smart smartphone plan will be able to choose from the widest range of 5G smartphones available from any UK network, starting from £69 per month. Alternatively, customers can choose an unlimited 5G SIM-only Smart plan for just £44 per month with the same benefits.

Customers who want access to the UK’s biggest and fastest 4G network can sign up for unlimited smartphone plans start from just £64 per month. 4G Smart Plan give customers two Swappable benefits, so they can choose the perks that best suits them at the start of their plan and then swap them for any of the other available benefits as their needs change. Swapping benefits is easy - customers simply switch online or via the My EE app.

EE is making unlimited data available to 4G SIM-only customers too, with prices starting from £34 per month for unlimited data on a 4G SIM-only plan and £39 for unlimited data on a 4G Smart SIM-only plan, which comes with two Swappable benefits.

All EE unlimited 4G and 5G data plan customers get the fastest speeds EE is able to offer and customers can use their plan to tether to other devices. What’s more, all of EE’s unlimited plans come with a 100GB monthly giftable data allowance, so customers can gift their data to additional lines linked to the account, and this increases to 120GB of giftable data if taking a 5G Smart handset plan.

extraction.body: T-Mobile is launching new “T-Mix” plans that bundle wireless service with subscriptions to services like Netflix, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, device promotions, and more, as reported earlier by Fierce Network. The Standard plan starts at $55 / month (with autopay) for one line and one “Pick,” which you can change up to four times during the year without changing the cost of your plan. Meanwhile, the mid-tier More plan starts at $75 / month for one line, two Picks per line, and unlimited data. The Loaded plan also comes with the same up to 4K UHD video streaming benefit, as well as up to 250GB of high-speed hotspot data and up to 30GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico. The types of perks you can add vary depending on how many your plan supports: * One Pick: Apple TV, DashPass by DoorDash, Google AI Plus, Hulu with ads, Netflix Standard with ads, Pandora Plus, Paramount Plus Essential, SiriusXM All Access (app only), YouTube Premium Lite, 500 miles / month through Delta SkyMiles, T-Satellite * Two Picks: Apple Music Individual, Google AI Pro, Pandora Premium, Xbox Game Pass Premium, YouTube Premium * Three Picks: Netflix Standard, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate * Four Picks: ESPN Unlimited, Netflix Premium As noted by CNET, you can also trade your Picks for discounts on a new phone. T-Mobile says that you can change up your perks every 90 days, according to Fierce Network. However, T-Mobile notes that how often you can change your perks depends on the benefit that you choose. “Some benefits let you switch any time, others hold your Picks for a quarter or longer,” T-Mobile says, adding that some services will charge if you switch them outside the change window. T-Mobile also offers an annual selection period where you can reset all of your perks.

passages: Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion .

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI.
SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.
The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model.
Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own.
In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses.

The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June .
Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.
The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise.
It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology.

"We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble.

We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.
In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.
U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.
Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models.
Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.
In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a " supply chain risk " — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries.
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice , with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

extraction.body: The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever. Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion . That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June . Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range. The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely. Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks . Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said. In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before. Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year. In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem." U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement. The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology. The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice , with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns. "Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University. But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible. With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading. In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion. Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation. The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation. Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to " pace the frontier ," or to slow the development of their most capable models. Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a " supply chain risk " — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks .

Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."
U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice , with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.

But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.
In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.

Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.

Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to " pace the frontier ," or to slow the development of their most capable models.

Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.

In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a " supply chain risk " — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.

extraction.body: The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever. Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion . That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June . Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range. The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely. Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks . Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said. In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before. Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year. In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem." U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement. The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology. The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice , with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns. "Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University. But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible. With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading. In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion. Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation. The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation. Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to " pace the frontier ," or to slow the development of their most capable models. Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a " supply chain risk " — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.

For the last few years, through a little-known program called Kronos, the Space Force has been consolidating and modernizing its suite of legacy systems that provide satellite operators with intelligence tools and command-and-control capabilities.
Now, USSF is reaching out to commercial firms to prototype and integrate new battle management tools on a faster and more continuous cadence to match the growing threats in orbit.

In a Nov. 12 commercial solutions opening , the Space Force said it is looking for a “broad range of solutions” across three areas: command and control, battle management, and space intelligence. These include advanced cloud-native services and infrastructure, AI decision support tools, and a “space attack planning toolkit” meant to improve coordination between tactical and operational units and speed up decision-making processes.

The goal, according to a Space Systems Command spokesperson, is to “rapidly bring commercial innovation” to the existing Kronos suite, which is being used today by the National Space Defense Center, Space Force component commands, and the multinational Combined Space Operations Center. SSC declined to name specific companies involved with the effort but said the vendor list includes “a broad mix of industry partners,” some with more traditional defense backgrounds and some newer to the scene.

The effort aligns with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s newly released acquisition reforms, SSC said, including his push for the Pentagon to “embrace the 85 percent solution” and field operational capabilities to users in the field at a faster pace.

“It allows the program to continuously incorporate emerging technologies, keep pace with evolving threats, and deliver the data-driven capabilities operators need across the Space Force,” the spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The CSO operationalizes the department’s shift toward faster, commercially driven acquisition to deliver mission capabilities to our Guardians in a contested domain.”

The U.S. military in recent years has shifted from viewing space as a benign environment to a warfighting domain , a transformation driven largely by increased threats from spacefaring adversaries like China and Russia. Space Force officials have stressed that having an integrated battle management capability is required in order to operate in that environment. That’s especially true for major initiatives like the Golden Dome missile shield, which will require a seamless C2 network to protect the U.S.

Kronos plays a key role in the battle management mission, SSC said. The program is part of SSC’s Battle Management/Command, Control, Communications and Space Intelligence portfolio, which is part of the newly formed System Delta 85. The Space Force is using DOD’s Software Acquisition Pathway to acquire new capabilities, an acquisition approach created to streamline software procurement by incorporating commercial buying practices.

“The Kronos program supports this mission by consolidating legacy systems into a modern, integrated software suite that strengthens decision-making, accelerates planning and deconfliction, enhances targeting and intelligence workflows, and provides shared situational awareness across combatant commands,” the spokesperson said. “The Kronos program is modernizing how the Space Force commands and conducts operations in a contested space environment.”

Find out more at afa.org For the last few years, through a little-known program called Kronos, the Space Force has been consolidating and modernizing its suite of legacy systems that provide satellite operators with intelligence tools and command-and-control capabilities. Now, USSF is reaching out to commercial firms to prototype and integrate new battle management tools on a faster and more continuous cadence to match the growing threats in orbit. In a Nov. 12 commercial solutions opening , the Space Force said it is looking for a “broad range of solutions” across three areas: command and control, battle management, and space intelligence. These include advanced cloud-native services and infrastructure, AI decision support tools, and a “space attack planning toolkit” meant to improve coordination between tactical and operational units and speed up decision-making processes. The goal, according to a Space Systems Command spokesperson, is to “rapidly bring commercial innovation” to the existing Kronos suite, which is being used today by the National Space Defense Center, Space Force component commands, and the multinational Combined Space Operations Center. SSC declined to name specific companies involved with the effort but said the vendor list includes “a broad mix of industry partners,” some with more traditional defense backgrounds and some newer to the scene. The effort aligns with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s newly released acquisition reforms, SSC said, including his push for the Pentagon to “embrace the 85 percent solution” and field operational capabilities to users in the field at a faster pace. “It allows the program to continuously incorporate emerging technologies, keep pace with evolving threats, and deliver the data-driven capabilities operators need across the Space Force,” the spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The CSO operationalizes the department’s shift toward faster, commercially driven acquisition to deliver mission capabilities to our Guardians in a contested domain.” The U.S. military in recent years has shifted from viewing space as a benign environment to a warfighting domain , a transformation driven largely by increased threats from spacefaring adversaries like China and Russia. Space Force officials have stressed that having an integrated battle management capability is required in order to operate in that environment. That’s especially true for major initiatives like the Golden Dome missile shield, which will require a seamless C2 network to protect the U.S. Kronos plays a key role in the battle management mission, SSC said. The program is part of SSC’s Battle Management/Command, Control, Communications and Space Intelligence portfolio, which is part of the newly formed System Delta 85. The Space Force is using DOD’s Software Acquisition Pathway to acquire new capabilities, an acquisition approach created to streamline software procurement by incorporating commercial buying practices. “The Kronos program supports this mission by consolidating legacy systems into a modern, integrated software suite that strengthens decision-making, accelerates planning and deconfliction, enhances targeting and intelligence workflows, and provides shared situational awareness across combatant commands,” the spokesperson said. “The Kronos program is modernizing how the Space Force commands and conducts operations in a contested space environment.” Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. extraction.body: This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: Tumors beneath the surface of the liver can be difficult to locate during laparoscopic, or keyhole, surgery. The new technology uses augmented reality to overlay a 3D visualization of the tumor and other anatomical structures on the surgeon's camera view. The visualization is updated as the camera changes position. "We have brought together the geometric tools needed to show where the tumor would be visible if the liver were semitransparent," says Torbjörn Lundh, professor at the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. "You can think of it as a GPS inside the organ. Instead of just having a map before surgery, we get continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström, transplant surgeon and head of the Transplant Centre at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. In June 2026, the technology was used in surgery on a patient for the first time. "The system could be used as planned during the operation, and the workflow worked well. The patient was able to go home the following day," says Kvarnström. To use the technology, the surgeon places a special sticker on the surface of the liver. The sticker is approximately one square centimeter (0.16 square inches) in size and has a QR code. As long as the camera can see the marker, the system can show the tumor or other structures beneath the surface. "The sticker acts as an artificial landmark on the surface of the liver, which is otherwise as smooth and even as a polished floor. Put very simply, the marker, together with the camera's position and the X-ray image taken before surgery, helps us calculate where the tumor should appear. That information can then easily be overlaid on the camera view," says Lundh. Further liver operations are planned for fall 2026. In parallel, work continues on clinical validation, product development, quality management systems and the steps required to obtain regulatory approval. In the longer term, a larger international study is planned in collaboration with the Intervention Centre at Oslo University Hospital and hospitals in Washington. Although the first clinical application has been in liver surgery, the researchers also see potential in other areas. "Our next major step is to make the method more widely applicable to other laparoscopic procedures. This is a new project that we have just started together with Chalmers Next Labs," says Lundh. "This technology can be used in many routine procedures, for tumors in other organs or to keep track of a particular anatomical structure. We are starting with liver surgery, but in the longer term the technology could have much broader applications," says Kvarnström. The collaboration behind the technology began 10 years ago, when surgeons Kvarnström and Mårten Falkenberg contacted mathematicians Lundh and Klas Modin. "This is an excellent example of research rooted in a real need in the operating room. Together with our master's thesis students, Klas and I have used and developed the mathematics needed to see where the tumor is hidden," says Lundh. He emphasizes the importance of collaboration across professional boundaries. "We hope our collaboration shows that really good things can happen when doctors and mathematicians work together in interdisciplinary teams that focus on the problem rather than the scientific tools, and where team members have a high degree of trust in one another and curiosity about each other's work," says Lundh. extraction.body: A research collaboration in Gothenburg has developed technology that creates an interactive 3D image of an organ during surgery. This makes it easier, for example, to remove a tumor that would otherwise remain hidden beneath the organ's surface. With the new technology, the surgeon places a small sticker with a QR code on the organ being operated on. So far, the technology has only been tested on the liver. As long as the camera can track the marker, the surgeon can see tumors and other structures beneath the surface. "It is a bit like having GPS navigation inside the organ. Instead of simply having a map before surgery, we receive continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström. He is a transplant surgeon and Head of the Transplant Center at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. Niclas Kvarnström, researcher, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg The new technology links a three-dimensional image of the patient's anatomy to the surgical field and displays it in relation to the surgeon's camera view. Using augmented reality, tumors, blood vessels, and other anatomical structures hidden beneath the organ's surface can be made visible to the surgeon directly in the surgical field. The information is continuously updated as the camera changes position. "This means that computer-generated content is overlaid on the physical world. It is a bit like Pokémon GO, but with much greater precision." Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: Tumors beneath the surface of the liver can be difficult to locate during laparoscopic, or keyhole, surgery. The new technology uses augmented reality to overlay a 3D visualization of the tumor and other anatomical structures on the surgeon's camera view. The visualization is updated as the camera changes position. "We have brought together the geometric tools needed to show where the tumor would be visible if the liver were semitransparent," says Torbjörn Lundh, professor at the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. "You can think of it as a GPS inside the organ. Instead of just having a map before surgery, we get continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström, transplant surgeon and head of the Transplant Centre at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. In June 2026, the technology was used in surgery on a patient for the first time. "The system could be used as planned during the operation, and the workflow worked well. The patient was able to go home the following day," says Kvarnström. To use the technology, the surgeon places a special sticker on the surface of the liver. The sticker is approximately one square centimeter (0.16 square inches) in size and has a QR code. As long as the camera can see the marker, the system can show the tumor or other structures beneath the surface. "The sticker acts as an artificial landmark on the surface of the liver, which is otherwise as smooth and even as a polished floor. Put very simply, the marker, together with the camera's position and the X-ray image taken before surgery, helps us calculate where the tumor should appear. That information can then easily be overlaid on the camera view," says Lundh. Further liver operations are planned for fall 2026. In parallel, work continues on clinical validation, product development, quality management systems and the steps required to obtain regulatory approval. In the longer term, a larger international study is planned in collaboration with the Intervention Centre at Oslo University Hospital and hospitals in Washington. Although the first clinical application has been in liver surgery, the researchers also see potential in other areas. "Our next major step is to make the method more widely applicable to other laparoscopic procedures. This is a new project that we have just started together with Chalmers Next Labs," says Lundh. "This technology can be used in many routine procedures, for tumors in other organs or to keep track of a particular anatomical structure. We are starting with liver surgery, but in the longer term the technology could have much broader applications," says Kvarnström. The collaboration behind the technology began 10 years ago, when surgeons Kvarnström and Mårten Falkenberg contacted mathematicians Lundh and Klas Modin. "This is an excellent example of research rooted in a real need in the operating room. Together with our master's thesis students, Klas and I have used and developed the mathematics needed to see where the tumor is hidden," says Lundh. He emphasizes the importance of collaboration across professional boundaries. "We hope our collaboration shows that really good things can happen when doctors and mathematicians work together in interdisciplinary teams that focus on the problem rather than the scientific tools, and where team members have a high degree of trust in one another and curiosity about each other's work," says Lundh. sources.title: Strategy pauses bitcoin (BTC) buys before Tuesday earnings - CoinDesk
passages: The pause is only the second this year for Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, which has turned itself into the largest publicly traded bitcoin treasury company and one of the most closely watched proxies for institutional BTC exposure.
The company last skipped a weekly purchase during the week of March 23 to March 29.
Strategy currently holds 818,334 BTC , equal to nearly 3.9% of bitcoin’s fixed 21 million supply.
Its most recent purchase added 3,273 BTC at an average price of $77,906 per bitcoin.
BTC was trading near $80,100 in Asian morning hours Monday, up about 20% over the past month.
The pause may seem a non-event but comes ahead of Strategy's first-quarter results Tuesday, with some Wall Street analysts expecting a loss of $18.98 per share.
Strategy is no longer valued as a software company with a bitcoin position, but as a bitcoin financing vehicle that happens to provide business intelligence software.
That means Tuesday’s report may be judged more on the durability of Saylor’s capital-raising machine and less for true operating performance.
Saylor says the buying resumes next week, but Tuesday’s earnings will show how much confidence investors still have in the machinery that makes that possible.
The company raised $82 million through the sale of common stock, according to Monday's 8-K filing , however, with no corresponding bitcoin purchases disclosed.
Strategy is expected to report first-quarter revenue of about $125 million, according to Yahoo Finance data from six analysts, up roughly 12.6% from $111.1 million a year earlier.

That would mark an improvement from the same quarter last year, when sales fell 3.6%, and suggests the underlying software business is still grinding higher even as the company’s identity is now almost entirely tied to bitcoin.

The pitch is yield backed by Strategy’s balance sheet and bitcoin-heavy capital strategy, but a going concern is that the product can start to look less like stable income and more like credit risk if market sentiment turns.
Strategy is taking a breather from buying bitcoin.
Higher bitcoin prices support Strategy’s valuation which improves its ability to raise capital, which funds more bitcoin purchases.
However, when sentiment weakens, the same structure gets more fragile.
No buys this week. Back to work next week. $BTC pic.twitter.com/lqliYZPAf4

The pause is only the second this year for Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, which has turned itself into the largest publicly traded bitcoin treasury company and one of the most closely watched proxies for institutional BTC exposure. The company last skipped a weekly purchase during the week of March 23 to March 29.

Strategy currently holds 818,334 BTC , equal to nearly 3.9% of bitcoin’s fixed 21 million supply. Its most recent purchase added 3,273 BTC at an average price of $77,906 per bitcoin. BTC was trading near $80,100 in Asian morning hours Monday, up about 20% over the past month.
The pause may seem a non-event but comes ahead of Strategy's first-quarter results Tuesday, with some Wall Street analysts expecting a loss of $18.98 per share.

Strategy is expected to report first-quarter revenue of about $125 million, according to Yahoo Finance data from six analysts, up roughly 12.6% from $111.1 million a year earlier. That would mark an improvement from the same quarter last year, when sales fell 3.6%, and suggests the underlying software business is still grinding higher even as the company’s identity is now almost entirely tied to bitcoin.

Earnings are expected to be lower, however. Yahoo Finance’s shows an average estimate for a loss of $27.33 per share for the March quarter, while Zacks Research data points to an expected loss of $3.41 per share for the upcoming release.

Strategy is no longer valued as a software company with a bitcoin position, but as a bitcoin financing vehicle that happens to provide business intelligence software. That means Tuesday’s report may be judged more on the durability of Saylor’s capital-raising machine and less for true operating performance.
One product drawing attention is STRC, a perpetual preferred share designed to trade near $100 while paying a variable monthly dividend, currently around 11.5% annualized.

The pitch is yield backed by Strategy’s balance sheet and bitcoin-heavy capital strategy, but a going concern is that the product can start to look less like stable income and more like credit risk if market sentiment turns.

Higher bitcoin prices support Strategy’s valuation which improves its ability to raise capital, which funds more bitcoin purchases. However, when sentiment weakens, the same structure gets more fragile.

Saylor says the buying resumes next week, but Tuesday’s earnings will show how much confidence investors still have in the machinery that makes that possible. passages: Choosing between Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) in 2026 requires balancing the high-growth potential of a cloud software leader against the steady reliability of a diversified technology veteran.
The company serves a diverse global client base, ranging from small businesses to large governments, across more than 175 countries.
About 60% of its total revenue is generated outside the United States, showcasing its deep reach into international markets and its reliance on a global network of partners.
The company competes with other software and consulting giants like Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SAP (NYSE:SAP), and Microsoft .

Additionally, the complexity of its global operations leaves it vulnerable to currency-exchange-rate volatility and the challenges of integrating smaller specialized acquisitions into its massive corporate structure.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Salesforce sells a comprehensive suite of cloud-based tools that allow companies to manage sales, customer service, and marketing on a single platform.
The business focuses on driving adoption across its various software modules, particularly among large enterprise clients.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x.
This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, and a lower number indicates a more conservative use of borrowed money.
The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, stood at roughly 0.8x.
Free cash flow for the period reached close to $14.4 billion.

Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow in the cash flow statement.
Over the last five years, the company has averaged 13.5% year-over-year revenue growth.
And while this gap has closed somewhat in recent quarters, Salesforce retains a more than 6% edge over IBM.
Another factor to consider is each company's profitability.
Investors might think that IBM would hold the advantage here, given its maturity relative to Salesforce.
In 2022, IBM's operating margin stood at around 12%, while Salesforce's was about 2%.
Given Salesforce's weak profitability from a few years ago, we'll examine each stock's price-to-sales (P/S) ratio.
In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Jan.
31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $41.5 billion.
This represents a growth rate of approximately 9.6% compared with the prior fiscal year.
Net income for this period climbed to roughly $7.5 billion.
This growth suggests the company is successfully upselling existing clients to more advanced tech stocks within its ecosystem.
In summary, these two tech stocks present an interesting contrast for investors.
Broadly speaking, their profitability is roughly equal.
Salesforce has an advantage in growth, while IBM holds an edge on valuation.
Therefore, in a head-to-head matchup, the choice likely comes down to investor temperament.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Salesforce wasn't one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
*Stock Advisor returns as of October 26, 2026.
Salesforce dominates the software landscape by helping companies manage customer data through the cloud.
IBM has transformed itself into a specialist in hybrid cloud and consulting.
Both companies are now competing for enterprise dollars by embedding artificial intelligence into their core service offerings.
Salesforce faces intense competition from established enterprise platforms and new start-ups that are native to artificial intelligence.

Operational risks include potential security breaches affecting sensitive customer data and the possibility that recent acquisitions, such as Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE), may not deliver the expected financial benefits.
The company must also navigate complex global regulations, including the EU AI Act, which could increase compliance costs and slow down the rollout of new software features.
When comparing IBM and Salesforce, investors should consider a few key factors.

facts.text: Choosing between Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) in 2026 requires balancing the high-growth potential of a cloud software leader against the steady reliability of a diversified technology veteran.
The company serves a diverse global client base, ranging from small businesses to large governments, across more than 175 countries.
About 60% of its total revenue is generated outside the United States, showcasing its deep reach into international markets and its reliance on a global network of partners.
The company competes with other software and consulting giants like Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SAP (NYSE:SAP), and Microsoft .

Additionally, the complexity of its global operations leaves it vulnerable to currency-exchange-rate volatility and the challenges of integrating smaller specialized acquisitions into its massive corporate structure.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Salesforce sells a comprehensive suite of cloud-based tools that allow companies to manage sales, customer service, and marketing on a single platform.
The business focuses on driving adoption across its various software modules, particularly among large enterprise clients.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x.
The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, stood at roughly 0.8x.
Free cash flow for the period reached close to $14.4 billion.

Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow in the cash flow statement.
Over the last five years, the company has averaged 13.5% year-over-year revenue growth.
And while this gap has closed somewhat in recent quarters, Salesforce retains a more than 6% edge over IBM.
Another factor to consider is each company's profitability.
Investors might think that IBM would hold the advantage here, given its maturity relative to Salesforce.
In 2022, IBM's operating margin stood at around 12%, while Salesforce's was about 2%.
Given Salesforce's weak profitability from a few years ago, we'll examine each stock's price-to-sales (P/S) ratio.
31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $41.5 billion.
This represents a growth rate of approximately 9.6% compared with the prior fiscal year.
Net income for this period climbed to roughly $7.5 billion.
This growth suggests the company is successfully upselling existing clients to more advanced tech stocks within its ecosystem.
In summary, these two tech stocks present an interesting contrast for investors.
Broadly speaking, their profitability is roughly equal.
Salesforce has an advantage in growth, while IBM holds an edge on valuation.
Therefore, in a head-to-head matchup, the choice likely comes down to investor temperament.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Salesforce wasn't one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
*Stock Advisor returns as of October 26, 2026.
Salesforce dominates the software landscape by helping companies manage customer data through the cloud.
IBM has transformed itself into a specialist in hybrid cloud and consulting.
Both companies are now competing for enterprise dollars by embedding artificial intelligence into their core service offerings.
Salesforce faces intense competition from established enterprise platforms and new start-ups that are native to artificial intelligence.

Operational risks include potential security breaches affecting sensitive customer data and the possibility that recent acquisitions, such as Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE), may not deliver the expected financial benefits.
The company must also navigate complex global regulations, including the EU AI Act, which could increase compliance costs and slow down the rollout of new software features.
When comparing IBM and Salesforce, investors should consider a few key factors.
Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Adobe, Arista Networks, International Business Machines, Microsoft, and Nvidia.
Choosing between a high-growth networking specialist and a legacy technology giant depends on your specific financial objectives.
Comparing these two reveals a classic trade-off between aggressive expansion in AI infrastructure and the steady, cash-generative stability of established enterprise software.
The company operates in more than 170 countries and partners with tech companies like Adobe and Microsoft to deliver enterprise solutions.
Its business model relies on deeply integrated relationships with large global organizations and government entities.
Arista Networks designs client-to-cloud networking products used in massive data centers.
The company serves a diverse group, including specialty cloud providers and financial institutions, but its growth is heavily tied to cloud titans.
Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as two specific end customers accounted for roughly 16% and 26% of total revenue in 2025.
The company also faces risks related to its pension obligations and the integration of new acquisitions, such as Logiq Consulting.
Geopolitical tensions and currency fluctuations can also impact its global revenue streams across the numerous countries where it operates.
Arista Networks has consistently reported high double-digit revenue growth, and the top-line growth rate accelerated last quarter, up 38% year over year.
This reflects a huge opportunity in the AI data center market.
Arista Networks faces risks from its heavy reliance on a small number of large customers, which can lead to volatile quarterly results.
The company is also vulnerable to supply chain issues in the semiconductor industry, as well as to competition from established networking providers like Cisco and Nvidia.
Since I favor stocks that offer the highest total return potential, regardless of dividends, I would buy Arista Networks.

Trailing-12-month (TTM) free cash flow through the second quarter of 2026 was approximately $5.2 billion, representing the cash generated after accounting for cash used to support operations and maintain capital assets.

sources.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
passages: In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20 times as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing.
The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working.

passages: Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads.

As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upwards of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.

Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.

Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.

“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides, but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers, and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20 times as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”

Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”

The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers…could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.
